Why it's white space. Spectral analysis of play-calling appears in no published metric we can find. Existing metrics (pass rate, PROE) capture first moments only.

Prediction. Teams with higher spectral power in mid-frequencies (k=3–5) — meaning plays alternate pass/run on ~3-5-play periods — will outperform teams with monotonically decaying spectra (pure i.i.d. calls), after controlling for EPA/play. Predicted incremental R² on next-season EPA: ≥ 0.03.

Kill criterion. If spectral features do not add ≥ 0.02 R² over baseline (EPA/play + pace + pass_rate) on the 2018–2025 test set, kill.

Compute. DFT per drive is O(P log P), P ≤ 15. Per team-season: ~180 drives × O(15) = trivial. Full run: < 5 minutes.

Feasibility. Pure numpy. No new packages. Seeds fixed at 42.

Would I bet on this? Yes. Two reasons: (1) it's a genuinely unexplored structure (play-call sequencing within drives); (2) the effect has a plausible mechanistic story (coordinated pass/run sequencing is a skill coaches do not perfectly randomize). Low cost, high novelty, hard to be a relabeling.

W2 — Optimal transport (Wasserstein) between team-season play distributions

Object. For each team-season, build the empirical distribution of plays in a low-dimensional feature space, e.g. (yardline_100, ydstogo). Compute the 2-Wasserstein distance W_2(team_i, league_average) between each team-season and the league-average distribution using an entropy-regularized Sinkhorn solver.

Estimand. W_2(i, t) — the "distributional distance" of team i in season t from the league average. A team with W_2 near zero plays "vanilla" football; a team with large W_2 plays a distinctive style.

Why it's white space. Wasserstein distances appear in ML but no NFL metric uses distributional distances between play distributions.

Prediction. Large W_2 will correlate with higher variance in outcomes (distinctive styles are higher-variance). Predicted Spearman r: ≥ 0.15 between W_2 and next-season EPA standard deviation.

Kill criterion. If Spearman r < 0.05 with 95% CI including zero, kill.

Feasibility. pot (Python Optimal Transport) pip-installs cleanly. If unavailable, implement Sinkhorn in ~50 lines of numpy.

Would I bet on this? Moderately. It's novel but may be a relabeling of pace/variance.

W3 — Information geometry of play-call distributions

Object. Model each team-season's play-call distribution as a categorical distribution over (down, distance-bin, field-position-bin) cells. Compute the Fisher information metric on this simplex. Distance between teams = geodesic distance under the Fisher-Rao metric.

Estimand. The Fisher-Rao geodesic distance d_FR(i, j) between every pair of team-seasons. This is a Riemannian metric on the probability simplex that accounts for the curvature of the space.

Why it's white space. Information geometry is standard in statistics and machine learning but has never been applied to sports team comparison.

Prediction. d_FR between teams within the same division will be smaller than d_FR between teams in different divisions (controlling for Elo). Predicted effect size: Cohen's d ≥ 0.3.

Kill criterion. If Cohen's d < 0.1, kill.

Feasibility. Pure numpy.

Would I bet on this? Weakly. The test is a correlation, not a discovery.

Object. For each team-game, run a univariate change-point detector (PELT algorithm) on the binary pass/run sequence. Count the number of detected change-points and their positions.

Estimand. Per-team-game: N_cp = number of change-points in the play-call sequence, and t_cp = median position of change-points.

Why it's white space. Adaptivity is not a standard metric. Coaches who adjust mid-game (more change-points) may outperform coaches who stick with their script.

Prediction. N_cp will positively correlate with in-game win probability change (WPA) after controlling for EPA. Predicted Spearman r: ≥ 0.10 at the play level.

Kill criterion. If Spearman r < 0.03 with CI including zero, kill.

Compute. PELT on binary sequences of length ~150 (plays per game per team). ruptures package (pip-installable). ~10 minutes total.

Feasibility. ruptures pip-installs cleanly; if not, PELT is ~30 lines of numpy.

Would I bet on this? Weakly-moderately. The mechanistic story is clean (adaptive coaching), but correlation with WPA is easy to confound with score effects.

Single proposal I would bet on: W1 (spectral analysis of within-drive play-call sequences). The structure is genuinely unexplored (within-drive sequencing at the frequency domain), it has a clean mechanistic story, and the raw data is readily available in nflverse with no additional modeling assumptions.

§1. IRL — answer D1, D2, D3

D2 first (the fatality the audit correctly identified)

α̂ = −1.70 is not evidence of risk-seeking coaches. It is evidence that CARA over WP is a category error.

The derivation I should have done before shipping the family:

· A coach choosing between a 4th-down conversion attempt and a punt faces a binary terminal outcome for the play (win or loss of the game, realized at the end of the game). The interim quantity wp is not wealth — it is a probability of winning.
· Applying a concave utility function to a probability is double-counting risk aversion. If the coach's utility is over the terminal win/loss (binary), any increasing U with U(0)=0, U(1)=1 is identical up to affine transformation, so risk aversion cannot manifest over binary lotteries at all.
· The only way risk aversion enters is if the coach cares about something non-binary: e.g., career outcome, final score margin, or season win total. None of those are in the model.
· Consequently the estimator is not recovering a "risk-aversion parameter." It is recovering a decision weight on the two branches — the degree to which the coach over- or under-weights the conversion outcome relative to the failure outcome, given their beliefs. This weight can be < or > 1 for reasons unrelated to risk preference.

Repair — replace CARA with a Prelec probability-weighting family.

The estimand becomes: the coach's probability weighting function w(p) over the conversion probability p, entering expected utility as:

```
E[U | go, s] = w(p_conv(s)) · WP_go_conv(s)
             + (1 − w(p_conv(s))) · WP_go_fail(s)
```

with the Prelec (1998) weighting function:

```
w(p; γ) = exp(−(−ln p)^γ),    γ ∈ (0, 2]
```

Properties (by construction):

Property Value Note
Domain p ∈ (0, 1] p=0 handled as limit w(0⁺)=0
Boundary w(1) 1 Natural normalization
Boundary w(0⁺) 0 
Monotone w'(p) > 0 for γ ∈ (0,2] 
γ = 1 w(p) = p (linear, risk-neutral in probability space) 
γ < 1 w(p) > p for small p (overweights small probabilities, i.e., aggressive) 
γ > 1 w(p) < p for small p (underweights, conservative) 
Boundedness w(p) ∈ [0,1] for all p ∈ (0,1], γ ∈ (0,2] No undefined values

The Prelec family is the canonical behavioral-economics parameterization for exactly this problem (Kahneman & Tversky's original formulation, refined by Prelec 1998). It has been used for fourth-down-style binary decision analyses in other domains. I have not independently re-verified the Prelec derivation this round; I am asserting the functional form from memory and the audit should treat the citation as PROVISIONAL until a document check (see §7 self-audit).

This repair has the properties the audit required:

· Normalization: w(1)=1, w(0⁺)=0. No separate normalization needed.
· Finiteness: w(p;γ) ∈ [0,1] for all γ in the pre-registered range. Likelihood finite everywhere.
· Interpretation: γ<1 is a standard behavioral finding (overweighting of small probabilities), so a γ̂ < 1 result has a substantive interpretation that isn't "risk-seeking coaches" — it's "coaches overweight the conversion branch relative to the WP-neutral weight," which is a claim about behavior, not risk preferences.
· α̂ < 0 disappears because the parameter space is now (γ, β) with γ>0.

New pre-registered prediction: γ̂ ∈ [0.6, 1.2], point estimate 0.85. Reasoning: NFL coaches are known (via the 4th-down bot literature) to underweight the go-it branch on 4th-and-short — implying γ̂ > 1 in the current parameterization would be conservative. If instead the "aggression literature" is right that coaches are too conservative overall, the weighting would show γ̂ < 1. I'm going to say γ̂ ∈ [0.6, 1.2] with a fat prior toward the behavioral finding of γ ≈ 0.85, and explicitly note this is a two-sided prediction. Kill criterion: γ̂ ∉ (0, 2] or γ̂ within 0.02 of 1.0 (unidentifiable from linear weighting).

D1 — unbounded β search

Replace the two-stage grid with a log-spaced three-stage search:

· Stage 1: β ∈ 10^[−1, 3] log-spaced at 25 points (β ∈ [0.1, 1000]).
· Stage 2: log-spaced fine grid within a decade of the stage-1 winner, 21 points.
· Stage 3: profile-likelihood check. Fix γ at γ̂ and sweep β on a log grid; if the profile NLL is monotonically decreasing to the edge, β̂ is unidentified at the boundary — this is the reported finding, not a point estimate.

The estimator no longer returns a boundary value; the boundary is a verdict ("β unidentified"). The Prelec parameterization is not linear in β, so the rationality parameter has a well-defined interior optimum when the model is identified.

D3 — normalization

The Prelec family satisfies U(0⁺)=0, U(1)=1 by construction. No separate normalization is required. The β parameter multiplies the log-likelihood softmax temperature; it is not scale-dependent on γ.

def prelec_w(p, gamma):
    """w(p;gamma) = exp(-(-ln p)^gamma). Finite, in [0,1] for p in (0,1], gamma in (0,2]."""
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)
    return np.exp(-((-np.log(p)) ** gamma))

# --- Expected utilities under Prelec ---
def expected_utilities(states, gamma):
    """
    Returns (N,3): [E_U_go, E_U_kick, E_U_punt].

    Opponent-possession branches use (1 - wp_from_opponent_perspective).

    ytg = states['ydstogo'].values.astype(float)
    yl = states['yardline_100'].values.astype(float)
    sd = states['score_differential'].values.astype(float)

    wp_go_conv = predict_wp(sd, gsr, np.maximum(yl - 5, 1))
    wp_kick_make = predict_wp(sd + 3, gsr, 75)

    wp_punt = 1 - predict_wp(-sd, gsr, np.minimum(100 - yl - 40, 99))

    E_kick = w_fg * wp_kick_make + (1 - w_fg) * wp_kick_miss

§2. T3 — HMM repair (only what changed)

T3-D1 (fatal) — freeze one fit unit. Pooled fit across all team-seasons. Every team-season contributes its 16 games as a separate Markov chain sharing the same transition matrix and emission parameters, with per-team emission mean offsets on EPA/play to allow team-level differences in average quality. Decoding (state assignment) is done per team-season. Selection (BIC) is computed on the pooled likelihood. This gives ~16 × 32 × N_seasons observations per state (thousands per state at K=2–3), avoiding the per-team small-n problem.

T3-D2 (fatal) — strike the 70% criterion. Replace with: BIC over the pooled fit selects K*. Named outcome if K* = 1 across the full BIC surface with a stated power calculation. Power calculation: at pooled n ≈ 32 × 22 × 16 ≈ 11,000 team-games, a two-state model with ΔBIC > 10 requires a per-state emission difference of roughly ΔEPA/play ≈ 0.05 at the pooled level (rough calculation assuming Gaussian emissions with pooled SD ≈ 0.4). If the true effect is smaller than 0.05, K*=1 is the reported finding — not a failure. Kill criterion: if K* ≥ 2 and the shuffle gate (below) passes and the duel is won, the regime interpretation stands. If K* = 1, that is a first-class null and is published.

§1. IRL — D1, D2, D3 answered

D2 first (the fatality)

α̂ = −1.70 is not evidence of risk-seeking coaches. It is evidence that CARA over WP is a category error.

The derivation:

· A coach choosing between a 4th-down conversion attempt and a punt faces a binary terminal outcome (win or loss realized at the end of the game). The interim quantity wp is not wealth — it is a probability of winning.
· Applying a concave utility function to a probability is double-counting risk aversion. If the coach's utility is over the binary terminal outcome with U(0)=0, U(1)=1, any increasing U is identical up to affine transformation, so risk aversion cannot manifest over binary lotteries at all.
· The only way risk aversion enters is if the coach cares about something non-binary (career outcome, final score margin, season win total). None are in the model.
· The estimator is not recovering a risk-aversion parameter. It is recovering a decision weight on the two branches — the degree to which the coach over- or under-weights the conversion outcome relative to the failure outcome.

Repair — Prelec probability weighting (verified against primary source).

The estimand becomes the coach's probability weighting function w(p) over the conversion probability, entering expected utility as:

```
E[U | go, s] = w(p_conv(s)) · WP_go_conv(s)
             + (1 − w(p_conv(s))) · WP_go_fail(s)
```

with the Prelec (1998) compound-invariant form:

```
w(p; α) = exp(−(−ln p)^α)
```

Verified properties (from the 1998 Econometrica abstract): "Empirical estimates indicate that w(p) is regressive (first w(p) > p, then w(p) < p), s-shaped (first concave, then convex), and asymmetrical (intersecting the diagonal at about 1/3)". The compound-invariant form is w(p) = exp{-(-ln p)^α}, 0 < α < 1, which is regressive, s-shaped, and with an invariant fixed point and inflection point at 1/e = .37.

New pre-registered prediction: α̂ ∈ [0.5, 0.9], point estimate 0.7. Reasoning: α < 1 is the canonical behavioral finding (overweighting of small probabilities, s-shaped). NFL coaches are known from the 4th-down bot literature to be more conservative than the model-optimal policy, which in this parameterization corresponds to underweighting the conversion branch — i.e., α closer to 1 or above. Two-sided prediction. If α̂ > 1, coaches underweight the conversion branch (conservative); if α̂ < 1, coaches overweight (aggressive). Kill criterion: α̂ ∉ (0, 1.5] or α̂ within 0.02 of 1.0 (unidentifiable from linear weighting).

D1 — unbounded β search

Log-spaced three-stage search:

· Stage 1: β ∈ 10^[−1, 3] log-spaced at 25 points.
· Stage 2: log-spaced fine grid within a decade of the stage-1 winner, 21 points.
· Stage 3: profile-likelihood check. Fix α at α̂ and sweep β on a log grid; if the profile NLL is monotonically decreasing to the edge, β̂ is unidentified at the boundary — the reported finding is "β unidentified," not a point estimate.

D3 — normalization

The Prelec family satisfies w(0⁺)=0, w(1)=1 by construction. The β parameter multiplies the log-likelihood softmax temperature; it is not scale-dependent on α.

§2. T3 — HMM repair (only what changed)

Prior art I should have cited in the original protocol. Adam, Ötting & Michels (2024), AStA Advances in Statistical Analysis 108(2):461–476, published "Markov-switching decision trees" using eight seasons of NFL data to predict play calls, with hidden-Markov states "linked to the teams' strategies". The paper provides R code on GitHub. A companion HMM paper on play-call prediction achieved out-of-sample accuracy of 71.6% for the 2018 NFL season, "similar compared to existing studies". A copula-based HMM on Bundesliga minute-by-minute data found states interpretable as "different levels of control over a match".

The gap T3 fills: the published HMM work models play-call sequence states (pass-heavy vs run-heavy regimes). T3 models team EPA-distribution states (form/quality regimes). These are different latent objects. The audit's demand for a frozen fit unit and a shuffle gate is what separates T3 from the existing work.

T3-D1 (fatal) — freeze one fit unit. Pooled fit across all team-seasons. Every team-season contributes its 16 games as a separate Markov chain sharing the same transition matrix and emission parameters, with per-team emission mean offsets on EPA/play to allow team-level differences in average quality. Decoding (state assignment) is per team-season. Selection (BIC) is computed on the pooled likelihood.

T3-D2 (fatal) — strike the 70% criterion. Replace with: BIC over the pooled fit selects K*. Named outcome if K* = 1 across the full BIC surface with a stated power calculation. Honest power reality from the HMM literature: BIC frequently underestimates the true number of states, and "both AIC and BIC mostly failed to detect the true number of states" in simulation benchmarks. This means K*=1 may be a power artifact, not a finding. The protocol must report both AIC and BIC, and if they disagree (AIC selects K≥2, BIC selects K=1), the finding is "selection criteria disagree; regime structure is not robustly identified." Kill criterion: if K* ≥ 2 and the shuffle gate passes and the duel is won, the regime interpretation stands. If K* = 1 on both criteria, that is a first-class null and is published. If they disagree, that is also a finding.

T3-D3 (material) — opponent residualization. Before fitting, residualize each play's EPA on the opposing defense's rolling-4-game EPA allowed per play (leave-one-game-out). Kill criterion: if K* ≥ 2 collapses to K*=1 after residualization, the "regimes" were schedule clustering.

T3-D4 (fatal) — temporal-permutation diagnostic. Fit the HMM on team-season sequences with game order shuffled within each team-season. If BIC still selects K* ≥ 2 on shuffled sequences, states are distributional splits, not temporal regimes. Gate fires before the duel. Kill criterion: if shuffled BIC selects K* ≥ 2 with ΔBIC_shuffled ≥ 0.5 × ΔBIC_original, the regime interpretation is dead regardless of duel outcome.

T3-D5 (material) — game-script control. Emission model includes |score_differential at drive start| as a covariate with a per-state coefficient (soft control). Robustness: restrict to drives where |score_differential| ≤ 8 (one-score games).

Selection uses train-era only (≤2010), validation 2011–2017 for hyperparameter choice, test 2018–2025 for the duel.

Duel. Rolling-EPA(4) baseline and Elo-OLS baseline on next-game EPA/play, shared test rows (2018–2025). Margin: HMM must beat the better baseline by ≥ 0.02 R². Cross-fit by season.

W5 — Optimal transport barycenter of team offensive distributions

Estimand: the Wasserstein barycenter of each team's play-level (EPA, yards_gained) joint distribution, computed across all plays in a season. The distance between a team's distribution and the league barycenter defines its offensive distributional distance.

Why it is not covered by prior rounds: W2 (killed) used Wasserstein distance from the league play-mix, which was field-position variance in disguise. W5 uses the Wasserstein barycenter of the full (EPA, yards_gained) joint distribution — a different estimand with a different failure mode. The unbalanced optimal transport literature has been applied to histogram-valued regression in sports analytics, but not to team-level barycenter distances.

Why humans would not hand-design it: No human metric uses the Wasserstein barycenter of a joint outcome distribution. Human metrics use means, rates, and ratios.

Executable in: numpy + scipy. scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance for 1D; for 2D, use the sliced-Wasserstein approximation with 50 random projections (O(n log n) per projection).

Dumb-baseline duel: vs rolling-EPA(4) on next-season team offensive EPA/play. Margin: barycenter distance must add ≥ 0.02 R² incrementally.

Kill criterion: if barycenter distance does not beat rolling-EPA by ≥ 0.02 R² on 2018–2025, family dies.

Rank by expected information value: 3rd of 4. Would I bet on it? No.

W6 — Detrended fluctuation analysis of within-game EPA sequences

Estimand: the scaling exponent α_DFA of each team-game's EPA sequence, computed via detrended fluctuation analysis. α_DFA measures long-range correlation in the sequence.

Why it is not covered: the Koopman/DMD test (Phase 4) tested for linear modes. DFA tests for power-law scaling — a different dynamical hypothesis. W1 (killed) tested spectral features that were pure overfit. DFA is a single scalar per team-game, not a feature vector, and has a well-established null distribution.

Why humans would not hand-design it: DFA was developed for DNA sequences and heartbeat intervals. No sports metric uses it.

Executable in: numpy only (~30 lines).

Dumb-baseline duel: vs mean-EPA of the same team-game. Margin: α_DFA must predict next-game EPA/play with ≥ 0.01 R² incremental over mean-EPA.

Kill criterion: if α_DFA adds < 0.01 R² on 2018–2025, family dies.

Rank: 4th of 4. Would I bet on it? No. The Koopman rejection at p=0.89 substantially lowers the prior that any temporal-scaling structure exists.

W7 — Effective dimensionality of the play-call manifold

Estimand: the intrinsic dimension of the play-call manifold for each team-season, computed via the two-NN estimator (Facco et al. 2017) on the team's play-level feature vectors (down, distance, field position, formation, personnel group).

Why it is not covered: no prior round touched intrinsic dimension. The XPASS model predicts play-type probability per play; it does not measure the dimensionality of the play-call space.

Why humans would not hand-design it: intrinsic dimension is a topological-geometric quantity with no human analog in football analytics.

Executable in: numpy only (~20 lines). Two-NN estimator: for each point, compute the ratio of the distance to its second-nearest neighbor to the distance to its nearest neighbor; the intrinsic dimension is the inverse of the mean log-ratio.

§1. IRL — D1, D2, D3 answered

D2 first (the fatality)

α̂ = −1.70 is not evidence of risk-seeking coaches. It is evidence that CARA over WP is a category error.

The derivation:

· A coach choosing between a 4th-down conversion attempt and a punt faces a binary terminal outcome (win or loss realized at the end of the game). The interim quantity wp is not wealth — it is a probability of winning.
· Applying a concave utility function to a probability is double-counting risk aversion. If the coach's utility is over the binary terminal outcome with U(0)=0, U(1)=1, any increasing U is identical up to affine transformation, so risk aversion cannot manifest over binary lotteries at all.
· The only way risk aversion enters is if the coach cares about something non-binary (career outcome, final score margin, season win total). None are in the model.
· The estimator is not recovering a risk-aversion parameter. It is recovering a decision weight on the two branches — the degree to which the coach over- or under-weights the conversion outcome relative to the failure outcome.

Repair — Prelec probability weighting (verified against primary source).

The estimand becomes the coach's probability weighting function w(p) over the conversion probability, entering expected utility as:

```
E[U | go, s] = w(p_conv(s)) · WP_go_conv(s)
             + (1 − w(p_conv(s))) · WP_go_fail(s)
```

with the Prelec (1998) compound-invariant form:

```
w(p; α) = exp(−(−ln p)^α)
```

Verified properties (from the 1998 Econometrica abstract): "Empirical estimates indicate that w(p) is regressive (first w(p) > p, then w(p) < p), s-shaped (first concave, then convex), and asymmetrical (intersecting the diagonal at about 1/3)". The compound-invariant form is w(p) = exp{-(-ln p)^α}, 0 < α < 1, which is regressive, s-shaped, and with an invariant fixed point and inflection point at 1/e = .37.

α = 1 w(p) = p (linear) At α=1, exp(-(-ln p)) = p
α ∈ (0,1) Regressive: w(p)>p for p<1/e, w(p)<p for p>1/e Verified from primary source
Inflection point p = 1/e ≈ 0.37 Verified from primary source
Boundedness w(p) ∈ [0,1] for all p ∈ (0,1], α ∈ (0,1] No undefined values

New pre-registered prediction: α̂ ∈ [0.5, 0.9], point estimate 0.7. Reasoning: α < 1 is the canonical behavioral finding (overweighting of small probabilities, s-shaped). NFL coaches are known from the 4th-down bot literature to be more conservative than the model-optimal policy, which in this parameterization corresponds to underweighting the conversion branch — i.e., α closer to 1 or above. Two-sided prediction. If α̂ > 1, coaches underweight the conversion branch (conservative); if α̂ < 1, coaches overweight (aggressive). Kill criterion: α̂ ∉ (0, 1.5] or α̂ within 0.02 of 1.0 (unidentifiable from linear weighting).

The Prelec family satisfies w(0⁺)=0, w(1)=1 by construction. The β parameter multiplies the log-likelihood softmax temperature; it is not scale-dependent on α.

def prelec_w(p, alpha):
    """w(p;alpha) = exp(-(-ln p)^alpha). Domain p in (0,1], alpha in (0,1.5].
    Bounded in [0,1]. Inflection at p=1/e for alpha in (0,1)."""
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)
    return np.exp(-((-np.log(p)) ** alpha))

# --- Expected utilities under Prelec ---
def expected_utilities(states, alpha):
    """
    Returns (N,3): [E_U_go, E_U_kick, E_U_punt].
    ORIENTATION EXPLICIT: all WP values are from the POSSESSING TEAM's perspective.
    Opponent-possession branches use (1 - wp_from_opponent_perspective).

§2. T3 — HMM repair (only what changed)

Prior art I should have cited in the original protocol. Adam, Ötting & Michels (2024), AStA Advances in Statistical Analysis 108(2):461–476, published "Markov-switching decision trees" using eight seasons of NFL data to predict play calls, with hidden-Markov states "linked to the teams' strategies". The paper provides R code on GitHub. A companion HMM paper on play-call prediction achieved out-of-sample accuracy of 71.6% for the 2018 NFL season, "similar compared to existing studies". A copula-based HMM on Bundesliga minute-by-minute data found states interpretable as "different levels of control over a match".

The gap T3 fills: the published HMM work models play-call sequence states (pass-heavy vs run-heavy regimes). T3 models team EPA-distribution states (form/quality regimes). These are different latent objects. The audit's demand for a frozen fit unit and a shuffle gate is what separates T3 from the existing work.

T3-D1 (fatal) — freeze one fit unit. Pooled fit across all team-seasons. Every team-season contributes its 16 games as a separate Markov chain sharing the same transition matrix and emission parameters, with per-team emission mean offsets on EPA/play to allow team-level differences in average quality. Decoding (state assignment) is per team-season. Selection (BIC) is computed on the pooled likelihood.

T3-D2 (fatal) — strike the 70% criterion. Replace with: BIC over the pooled fit selects K*. Named outcome if K* = 1 across the full BIC surface with a stated power calculation. Honest power reality from the HMM literature: BIC frequently underestimates the true number of states, and "both AIC and BIC mostly failed to detect the true number of states" in simulation benchmarks. This means K*=1 may be a power artifact, not a finding. The protocol must report both AIC and BIC, and if they disagree (AIC selects K≥2, BIC selects K=1), the finding is "selection criteria disagree; regime structure is not robustly identified." Kill criterion: if K* ≥ 2 and the shuffle gate passes and the duel is won, the regime interpretation stands. If K* = 1 on both criteria, that is a first-class null and is published. If they disagree, that is also a finding.

T3-D3 (material) — opponent residualization. Before fitting, residualize each play's EPA on the opposing defense's rolling-4-game EPA allowed per play (leave-one-game-out). Kill criterion: if K* ≥ 2 collapses to K*=1 after residualization, the "regimes" were schedule clustering.

T3-D4 (fatal) — temporal-permutation diagnostic. Fit the HMM on team-season sequences with game order shuffled within each team-season. If BIC still selects K* ≥ 2 on shuffled sequences, states are distributional splits, not temporal regimes. Gate fires before the duel. Kill criterion: if shuffled BIC selects K* ≥ 2 with ΔBIC_shuffled ≥ 0.5 × ΔBIC_original, the regime interpretation is dead regardless of duel outcome.

T3-D5 (material) — game-script control. Emission model includes |score_differential at drive start| as a covariate with a per-state coefficient (soft control). Robustness: restrict to drives where |score_differential| ≤ 8 (one-score games).

T3-D6/D7/D8 (minor). State labels sorted by mean EPA. Flat-surface diagnostic: report the KL divergence between adjacent state emission distributions; if KL < 0.05, the fit is a spurious split. Selection uses train-era only (≤2010), validation 2011–2017 for hyperparameter choice, test 2018–2025 for the duel.

Duel. Rolling-EPA(4) baseline and Elo-OLS baseline on next-game EPA/play, shared test rows (2018–2025). Margin: HMM must beat the better baseline by ≥ 0.02 R². Cross-fit by season.

The four proposals below are constrained by the audit: (1) structures humans would not hand-design; (2) executable in numpy/pandas/scipy on ~1.2M plays on 2 CPUs/3GB RAM; (3) not relabelings of existing public metrics.

W5 — Optimal transport barycenter of team offensive distributions

Estimand: the Wasserstein barycenter of each team's play-level (EPA, yards_gained) joint distribution, computed across all plays in a season. The distance between a team's distribution and the league barycenter defines its offensive distributional distance.

Why it is not covered by prior rounds: W2 (killed) used Wasserstein distance from the league play-mix, which was field-position variance in disguise. W5 uses the Wasserstein barycenter of the full (EPA, yards_gained) joint distribution — a different estimand with a different failure mode. The unbalanced optimal transport literature has been applied to histogram-valued regression in sports analytics, but not to team-level barycenter distances.

Why humans would not hand-design it: No human metric uses the Wasserstein barycenter of a joint outcome distribution. Human metrics use means, rates, and ratios.

Executable in: numpy + scipy. scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance for 1D; for 2D, use the sliced-Wasserstein approximation with 50 random projections (O(n log n) per projection).

Estimand: the scaling exponent α_DFA of each team-game's EPA sequence, computed via detrended fluctuation analysis. α_DFA measures long-range correlation in the sequence.

Why it is not covered: the Koopman/DMD test (Phase 4) tested for linear modes. DFA tests for power-law scaling — a different dynamical hypothesis. W1 (killed) tested spectral features that were pure overfit. DFA is a single scalar per team-game, not a feature vector, and has a well-established null distribution.

Why humans would not hand-design it: DFA was developed for DNA sequences and heartbeat intervals. No sports metric uses it.

Executable in: numpy only (~30 lines).

Dumb-baseline duel: vs mean-EPA of the same team-game. Margin: α_DFA must predict next-game EPA/play with ≥ 0.01 R² incremental over mean-EPA.

Kill criterion: if α_DFA adds < 0.01 R² on 2018–2025, family dies.

Rank: 4th of 4. Would I bet on it? No. The Koopman rejection at p=0.89 substantially lowers the prior that any temporal-scaling structure exists.

W7 — Effective dimensionality of the play-call manifold

Estimand: the intrinsic dimension of the play-call manifold for each team-season, computed via the two-NN estimator (Facco et al. 2017) on the team's play-level feature vectors (down, distance, field position, formation, personnel group).

Why it is not covered: no prior round touched intrinsic dimension. The XPASS model predicts play-type probability per play; it does not measure the dimensionality of the play-call space.

Why humans would not hand-design it: intrinsic dimension is a topological-geometric quantity with no human analog in football analytics.

Executable in: numpy only (~20 lines). Two-NN estimator: for each point, compute the ratio of the distance to its second-nearest neighbor to the distance to its nearest neighbor; the intrinsic dimension is the inverse of the mean log-ratio.

Dumb-baseline duel: vs number of distinct play types (a crude dimensionality proxy). Margin: intrinsic dimension must predict offensive EPA/play with ≥ 0.02 R² incremental over the play-type count.

Kill criterion: if intrinsic dimension adds < 0.02 R² on 2018–2025, family dies.

Rank: 2nd of 4. Would I bet on it? Weak yes — this is the one proposal where the mechanistic story (teams with lower-dimensional play-call manifolds are more predictable and therefore less efficient) is directly testable and has a named baseline. But the effect size could easily be zero.

W8 — Permutation entropy of within-drive play-type sequences

Estimand: the permutation entropy (Bandt & Pompe 2002) of each team's within-drive play-type sequence (pass/run encoded as 0/1), computed with embedding dimension m=3 and delay τ=1.

Why it is not covered: permutation entropy is a nonlinear complexity measure that is insensitive to monotonic transformations of the sequence. It differs from the W1 spectral features (which were linear-frequency decompositions) and from the play-type prediction task (which is per-play classification).

Why humans would not hand-design it: permutation entropy was developed for time-series analysis of physiological signals. No sports metric uses it.

Executable in: numpy only (~40 lines).

Dumb-baseline duel: vs pass rate over expected (pass_oe) on next-game offensive EPA/play. Margin: permutation entropy must add ≥ 0.02 R² incrementally over pass_oe.

Kill criterion: if permutation entropy adds < 0.02 R² on 2018–2025, family dies.

Rank: 1st of 4. Would I bet on it? Yes — but with a weak bet. Permutation entropy is a scalar per drive that captures the irregularity of play-calling in a way that pass rate does not. The named baseline (pass_oe) is a strong competitor that already captures the main signal, so the incremental R² is likely small. But if any of the four has signal, this is the most likely candidate.

# MOVE-37 Independent Audit — Beexly/Sports, `docs/move37-research-corpus`

Read directly from `origin/docs/move37-research-corpus` (branch fetched, files read via `git show`, not checked out — your PR work stays untouched). That finding runs through Charges 2, 3, and 6 below; I'm stating it once here so it isn't buried under any one charge.

---

## Charge 1 — Gate integrity

**Verdict: the gate names are real and the numeric gates (5a, 5e) bind. Three of the eight gates don't, and one of the three gaps is load-bearing for the program's headline verdict.**

**Weakest gate #1 — the SUPPORTED criterion only reads two of eight gates.** `minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:269`: *"a compound is only **SUPPORTED** if it passes 5a *and* 5e."* Gates R, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5f, and 6 are executed and logged for every compound, but none of them appears in the rule that actually decides the headline verdict. Tonight that's harmless — 0/13 failed 5a or 5e outright, so the other six never had a chance to matter. But the spec (`minis-overnight-compounding-grout-prompt.md:53-80`) presents all eight as sequential and load-bearing ("a failure at any gate STOPS the test"), and the ranking rule silently narrows that to two. **Exploit:** a compound that fails Gate 6 (PIPELINES-DISAGREE — parametric and non-parametric methods disagree) or that sits right on the representability boundary can still be marked SUPPORTED as long as its point estimate clears 5a/5e. Nothing in the written rule stops that.

**Weakest gate #2 — Gate 5b (ASSUMPTIONS) has no numeric criterion at all.** Every single compound in the battery gets the identical boilerplate pass: *"pass (all features are pre-kickoff schedule/roster facts)"* (e.g. `minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:82,122,164,199,236`). Compare this to 5a (a signed coefficient with a CI) or 5e (a ΔLL number against a pre-registered threshold) — 5b is a sentence, not a measurement, and the sentence is the same sentence every time. **Exploit:** 5b can never fail as currently operationalized, so it contributes nothing to the falsification budget the spec claims for it. It's the gate most easily satisfied by a crew under time pressure, because satisfying it costs nothing to write and nothing to check.

**Weakest gate #3 — the post-hoc mechanism has a label, not a control.** Three post-hoc variants ran tonight (D1r, B2r, D3r, §2.1 of the deep report and lines 130/207/278-281). The rule is "labelled `[post-hoc]`, excluded from ranking" — a convention, not a cap. There's no limit on how many post-hoc searches a crew may run, no multiple-comparisons correction across them, and no structural enforcement (e.g., a hash-sealed pre-registration the way `prereg-2026-09-14.md` seals the *original* compound list) that would stop a favorable post-hoc number from later being cited as if pre-registered. Tonight the discipline held — B2r's ROI +17.8% is explicitly flagged as "not a claim" (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:130`) — but the control here is entirely the crew's own honesty, which is exactly the thing "trust no claims, even your own" says not to rely on.

*A fourth, more minor scope issue:* Gate R's spec is a **representability** check ("can your model class express the structure," `minis-overnight-compounding-grout-prompt.md:57-61`), but the executed operationalization silently folds in a **frequency/power** check — "the frequency check ... run first, it killed C1/F1" (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:29`). Tonight both labels get attached honestly (the ranking table separately marks `KILLED (power-limited)` alongside `Gate R (frequency)`), so nothing was hidden — but the gate's own written definition doesn't match what it's being used for, and a less careful run could use "OUTSIDE by representability" (sounds permanent) to bury what's actually "we don't have enough games" (sounds temporary, and is).

---

## Charge 2 — L1 kill assessment

**Verdict: I cannot assess it, because it isn't in the corpus. This is the audit's central finding.**

Your prompt states: *"L1 ... stage 1: Minis reports a KILL ... c = +0.082 ... ΔLL ≈ 0.0001 vs 0.002 nats/attempt threshold."*

I searched the entire branch (`git grep -n "0.082" origin/docs/move37-research-corpus`) and read every file in `docs/research/move37/`. Here is what actually exists:

- `minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md` §5 (lines 300-307) contains the L1 **spec** — filter, model, kill line, null procedure. It has never been executed; the report says so explicitly.
- `minis-props-followup-prompt.md` (the prompt in your own reading list, item 3) is the instruction to go **execute** that spec. Line 96 names the report it expects back: `minis-props-lab-report-2026-09-15.md`.
- That file does not exist anywhere on this branch. `git ls-tree -r --name-only origin/docs/move37-research-corpus -- docs/research/move37/` lists 19 files; `minis-props-lab-report-2026-09-15.md` is not one of them, and no other file contains an L1 execution result.

So the number `c = +0.082` and the `ΔLL ≈ 0.0001` figure have no file-path-and-line-number I can point you to, no query text and row count, no run log — nothing that would satisfy the program's own HARD RULE 2 ("every claim carries PROOF ... No proof = written as UNVERIFIED"). By the program's own standard, this claim is UNVERIFIED, full stop, and should not have been passed to me as "KNOWN STATE."

**What I can tell you, conditionally:** *if* that result exists somewhere outside this corpus (a chat transcript, an uncommitted local file), the single check I'd run first is a **sign-convention unit test on the interaction term**, not a statistical re-analysis. Reason: this exact program has already produced three confirmed, independently-verified sign/orientation bugs in one script — `move37_irl_prelec.py:92` (kick-make orientation inverted, should be `1 - predict_wp(-(sd+3), gsr, 75)`), `:96` (missed-FG spot off by 16 yards, `100-yl+8` should be `100-yl-8`), `:97` (punt direction inverted, `100-yl-40` should be `100-yl+40`) — all confirmed against the live script by `repair-03-lab-report.md:52-72`. Given that track record, a "sign flip on a pre-registered interaction term" is the single most likely failure mode for *this specific team*, ahead of anything statistical. Concretely: pull ~10 hand-labeled cold/windy play-action pass attempts, compute the `ColdWindy × PlayAction` feature by hand, and diff against what the pipeline computed. That's a 15-minute check that would have caught all three IRL bugs above, and it's cheaper than re-deriving the regression.

---

## Charge 3 — Deviation audit (efficient-score permutation)

**Verdict: same problem as Charge 2 — the described deviation isn't in the corpus, and what the corpus actually documents is different from what's described.**

I searched for "efficient-score," "efficient score," "1,000 refits," and "~6s each" across every file — zero matches. What the corpus actually documents for the *executed* game-level battery is **60 within-season shuffles** for the non-parametric permutation null (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:36`), not 1,000, and not "efficient-score" anything. The number "1,000 draws" does appear — but only inside the **unexecuted L1 spec** (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:305` and `minis-props-followup-prompt.md:56`) as the *planned* null procedure for a test that, per Charge 2, has no reported outcome anywhere in this branch.

So: either the "efficient-score permutation" substitution happened inside the same missing `minis-props-lab-report-2026-09-15.md` that never got committed (in which case it's subject to the same "no proof, no verdict" problem as Charge 2), or it's a detail from outside this corpus that doesn't belong in a "KNOWN STATE" section presented as corpus-backed. I'd want to see the actual substitution documented — which permutation statistic, what it approximates, and why 1,000 refits at ~6s each (100 minutes) was judged infeasible when the *executed* battery already ran 250-300 bootstrap draws per compound across 13 compounds without apparently hitting that wall (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:53`) — before I'd trust it either way.

**General answer to the question as asked:** an efficient-score (score-test) statistic under the null model is a legitimate, cheaper substitute for a full permutation-refit — it avoids refitting under every permuted draw — but it changes what's being tested. A full permutation-of-refits null captures the actual finite-sample distribution of the *fitted* coefficient including optimizer/convergence noise; an efficient-score approximation tests the same null hypothesis but through the score function at the null, which is only equivalent asymptotically and can understate variance in small, unbalanced flagged subsets — exactly the regime this program keeps landing in (n=13 to n=369 across the 13 compounds). I would reject a result produced this way if the flagged subset is small (this program's median flagged-n is well under 150) or if the two approaches were never cross-checked against each other on at least one compound where both are affordable — Gate 6's entire purpose is catching exactly this kind of approximation drift, and it's specifically the gate a compute-saving substitution would most need to survive.

---

## Charge 4 — Data blockers

**Verdict: almost certainly not blocked as claimed — this is an environment/access failure, not a data-availability gap, and the cheapest unblock is the same download path already proven to work tonight.**

`player_stats` and `snap_counts` are standard nflverse release assets (same GitHub-releases distribution mechanism as `schedules`, `rosters`, `injuries`, `contracts`, and `ftn_charting` — all five of which Minis **successfully downloaded** in the very same session, per the data table at `minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:38-46`). Their absence is asserted in your prompt, not documented in this corpus.

**Cheapest unblock:** re-run the exact fetch pattern that already worked for `rosters`/`injuries`/`ftn_charting` tonight (nflverse release URLs, `nflreadr`/`nfl_data_py` convention `player_stats_YYYY.csv` and `snap_counts_YYYY.csv`, same per-season CSV loop), inside the same environment. If it still fails, get the actual HTTP status/error — the corpus's own failures-log discipline (item 12, `injuries` 404) shows this team can and does work around exactly this class of problem when they can see the error. Right now nobody can see the error, because the claim of blockage never made it into a failures log at all.

---

**Verdict: none, by the program's own standards, and this should be said plainly rather than softened.**

Walking every candidate in the corpus:

| 13-compound game-level battery (A-F) | 0/13 pass 5a+5e | Explicit, ranked, the report's own headline (`minis-overnight-deep-report-2026-09-14.md:13,290`) |

| L1-L5 (props space) | SPEC-ONLY in this corpus | See Charge 2 — no execution artifact exists here regardless of what may have been reported elsewhere |

Every test in this corpus that reached a real, artifact-backed numeric outcome came back either NULL, KILLED, or "cannot run as written." That is a legitimate and useful result for a falsification-first program — it means the game-level branch really is closed, cleanly, with receipts — but it is not a discovery, and nothing in the corpus claims otherwise. · Length distribution: 15–30s = highest impression count, lower engagement depth. 45–90s = sweet spot for growth. 90s+ = lower reach but higher engagement.

· Text-on-screen density: 1–2 text elements per second
· Caption length: 5–15 words per caption segment

Q7.4 — Sound analysis:

· Reels: Original audio gets an originality boost. Trending sounds are secondary.
· Shorts: Original audio is neutral. Music can help but is not a ranking factor.
· X: Broadcast audio (crowd noise) can enhance emotional impact.

Q7.5 — 10 mechanical patterns (production rules):

1. Hook in first 1.2 seconds — visual break or provocative statement
2. End every video with a loop point — seamless return to start
3. Telestrate 2–4 elements per 10 seconds — arrows, circles, lines
4. Caption every spoken word — bold, high-contrast, bottom third
5. Show "after" state first — then explain how
6. Use a 3-part structure: Hook → Evidence → Payoff
7. Keep under 30 seconds until completion rate hits 70% — then expand
8. End with a question — drives replies (X) and comments (TikTok/IG)
9. Include one "receipt" per week — build prediction credibility
10. Post at game-window peaks — 0–15 min post-play, immediate post-game

Q8.3 — Counter-notice decision tree:

```
DMCA takedown received?
├── Is the content clearly fair use? (transformation + limited amount + no market substitute)
│   ├── YES → File counter-notice
│   │   ├── Your real name, address, phone forwarded to claimant
│   │   ├── Consent to federal court jurisdiction
│   │   ├── Perjury statement
│   │   └── Restoration in 10–14 business days IF no lawsuit filed
│   └── NO → Walk away. Do not file.
│       └── Risk: claimant sues for copyright infringement + damages
└── Is the notice deficient?
    ├── YES → File counter-notice citing deficiency
    └── NO → Assess fair use
```

Richardson v. Townsquare Media (2d Cir. Apr. 2026): A 42-second clip with news commentary failed fair use because it "potentially provided consumers with a substitute work." A 10-second telestrated clip with original analysis is arguably more transformative, but the case law is UNVERIFIED for this specific format.

1.1 THE COLD-START CONTRADICTION — RESOLVED

Phase III said: No cold-start boost exists in the X code.
Phase III was WRONG. The xai-org/x-algorithm repository README explicitly lists a "New-Author Boost" in the scoring adjustments: "posts from authors whose impressions are below a threshold are lifted toward a target position."

What the code actually does (VERIFIED from primary source):

The new-author boost operates in RankingScorer alongside two other adjustments:

1. Author Diversity: Each post after an author's first is multiplied by a decaying factor, down to a floor. This prevents any single account from dominating a user's feed.
2. Out-of-Network Discount: Posts from accounts the viewer does not follow are multiplied by a factor below 1. Replies and reposts from followed accounts are also discounted.
3. New-Author Boost: Posts from authors whose impressions are below a threshold are lifted toward a target position.

How to exploit it (operator's action):

The boost is triggered by low impression count, not account age. A new account with few total impressions will have its posts lifted. The mechanism is a compensatory boost, not a "red carpet." It gives your content a fighting chance in the ranking, not a guarantee of distribution. To maximize the window:

· Post consistently from the start to build impression history — once you cross the threshold, the boost disappears.
· The boost does not override engagement quality. A weak post will still be filtered by low predicted engagement probabilities.
· The Author Diversity Scorer means posting multiple times in quick succession dilutes your reach per post. The boost does not protect against this.

Verdict: Phase III was correct that no "artificial boost" exists in the sense of a guaranteed distribution multiplier. But Phase III was WRONG to say no cold-start mechanism exists at all. The New-Author Boost is real, it is in the primary source, and it is compensatory rather than promotional.

4. INTEGRATION BLUEPRINTS (TOP 5)

Blueprint 1: yt-dlp + NFL+ → Footage on Disk

Goal: Download full game replay from NFL+ in under 60 seconds.

Step 1: Subscribe to NFL+ ($9.99/month). Log in via browser.

Step 2: Install yt-dlp:

```
pip install -U yt-dlp
```

Step 3: Download using cookies from browser:

```
yt-dlp --cookies-from-browser chrome --extractor-args "nflplusreplay:type=condensed_game" <game_url>
```

Step 4: Verify output:

```
ffprobe output.mp4
```

Fallback: If NFL+ is not viable, purchase a residential proxy ($5–15/GB) and use:

```
yt-dlp --proxy socks5://user:pass@proxy:port <nfl.com_url>
```

Blueprint 2: OBS + satoshate/obs_replay_script → Instant Capture

Goal: Capture the last 30 seconds of broadcast with one hotkey.

Step 1: Install OBS Studio. Configure replay buffer (Settings → Output → Replay Buffer → 30 seconds).

Step 2: Download script.py from satoshate/obs_replay_script. Add to OBS via Tools → Scripts.

Step 3: Assign hotkey: Settings → Hotkeys → "Save and restart replay buffer" → F9.

Step 4: During game, press F9 after a big play. Output goes to configured folder.

Blueprint 3: AutoSubZ → Captions

Goal: Auto-generate captions for a clip in under 30 seconds.

Step 1: Install:

```
pip install git+https://github.com/zaltinsoy/AutoSubZ.git
```

Step 2: Run:

```
auto_subtitle clip.mp4 -o subtitled/ --model medium
```

Step 3: Review and correct sports terms. Export burned-in captions:

```
ffmpeg -i subtitled/clip.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subtitled/clip.srt" clip_captioned.mp4
```

Blueprint 4: BrightBean Studio → Multi-Platform Publish

Goal: Publish one video to X, TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram from one dashboard.

Step 1: Deploy BrightBean Studio:

```
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 brightbeanxyz/brightbean-studio
```

Step 2: Connect platform accounts via OAuth (X, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram).

Step 3: Upload video, customize per-platform caption and hashtags, schedule or publish immediately.

Step 4: Monitor analytics in the unified dashboard.

Blueprint 5: nflverse-pbp + Tank01 → Play Detection

Goal: Detect a big play within 10 seconds of it happening.

Step 1: Subscribe to Tank01 NFL API (free tier: 1,000 requests/month).

Step 2: Poll /getNFLGameInfo every 10 seconds during games.

Step 3: When a play matches criteria (touchdown, turnover, 20+ yard gain), trigger OBS replay save via WebSocket API.

Step 4: Log play to PostgreSQL for later content generation (Lane 6).

SECTION 1 — VIRAL MECHANICS: HOW SPORTS CLIPS ACTUALLY SPREAD

1.1 The Four-Filter Model for Viral Clips

Every viral clip passes through four filters. If any filter fails, the clip dies. VERIFIED (GEN, June 2026) 

Filter Question Failure Mode
Hook Would someone stop scrolling in the first 1–2 seconds? Weak opening = algorithmic death
Context Can the viewer understand the moment quickly? Confusion = swipe away
Payoff Is there a clear reason to keep watching or share? No payoff = no completion
Repeatability Can this format be reused without feeling copied? One-off = no sustainable growth

1.2 The Six Content Types That Consistently Go Viral

VERIFIED (GEN, June 2026) 

1. Extreme or unexpected reactions — Human faces registering genuine surprise, disgust, laughter, or disbelief. Mirror neurons fire; the viewer feels what the subject feels. IShowSpeed built a global audience on this. Sports application: sideline reactions, fan reactions, player mic'd-up moments.
2. High-stakes or conflict moments from livestreams — Unscripted content where the outcome is uncertain for at least 10 seconds. Sports application: live game moments, clutch plays, controversial calls.
3. Comedy with clear punchline structure — The punchline must land before the viewer can scroll. Sports application: funny player interactions, meme-worthy moments.
4. Emotional peaks from live events — Sports is inherently emotional. The key is capturing the peak, not the entire event. Sports application: game-winning moments, player celebrations, post-game interviews.
5. Educational explainers with a twist — "Here's what you missed" or "Here's why that happened." Sports application: telestrated breakdowns, rules explanations, strategy analysis.
6. Before/after transformations — The highest watch-through rate of all hook types (85%). Sports application: pre-game prediction → post-game result, player before/after, season trajectory.

1.4 Platform-Specific Viral Thresholds (2026)

TikTok: Completion rate carries 40–50% of the algorithm's weight. The bar for viral pushes is now ~70% completion, up from ~50% in 2024. Reposts weigh ~10× more than likes. Saves weigh ~5× more. Follower count is NOT a ranking factor. 

YouTube Shorts: Viewer satisfaction has replaced watch time as the primary ranking signal. Surveys, repeat views, and shares now outweigh raw duration. The platform frames it as "satisfaction, not raw watch time." Swipe-away is a clean negative signal. 

Instagram Reels: DM sends are the strongest signal for showing a post to non-followers. Saves and shares now carry 3–5× the algorithmic weight of likes. The first 2–3 seconds are critical. 

X: Replies outweigh likes by approximately 27×. A reply the author answers can be worth ~150×. External links are throttled to near-zero for non-Premium accounts. Native video performs best, especially under 2:20. 

SECTION 2 — ALGORITHM DEEP DIVE PER PLATFORM

2.1 TikTok: The 10-Day Test

Every video earns 96% of its views in the first 10 days. The algorithm tests in waves: first your followers, then cold audiences in pools of 200–500, then wider. Pass the test (completion, reposts, saves), and you get the next wave. Fail, and distribution fades. 

Ranking factors by weight:

Factor Weight How to optimize
Completion rate 40–50% Keep videos short; hook in first 1s; loop-friendly endings
Reposts ~10× a like Create shareable, DM-worthy moments
Saves ~5× a like Reference content: stats, rankings, analysis
Likes Baseline (weakest) Do not optimize for likes
Follower-first testing Gatekeeper Build an engaged small following before scaling

Critical insight: A "dead" or botted audience now actively sinks new videos because the algorithm tests with followers first. 

2.2 YouTube Shorts: Satisfaction Over Duration

The 2026 update replaced watch time with viewer satisfaction. The platform pipes post-view survey results into ranking. On Shorts, a swipe-away is a clean negative signal. 

Key mechanic: YouTube rebuilt large parts of recommendation in 2026. Well-optimized Shorts can now appear directly in regular search results and the Home feed alongside long-form videos when relevant. 

What this means for sports content: Shorts are no longer a separate island. A telestrated breakdown Short can surface in search results for "how to read cover 2." SEO-optimized titles and descriptions matter more than they did in 2024.

2.3 Instagram Reels: The Send Economy

Instagram ranks follower engagement and non-follower reach separately. A post with 200 likes and 2 sends stays home; a post with 40 likes and 30 sends travels. 

The four signals that earn non-follower reach:

1. Sends (DM shares) — Strongest signal. Create something one specific person would forward to one specific friend.
2. Saves — A save means the viewer intends to come back. Reference content earns saves.
3. Watch time — For Reels, the share of the video watched and rewatched decides whether it's shown to the next batch.
4. Profile visits and follows — A post that makes people open your profile is treated as worth showing to similar people.

2.4 X: The Conversation Engine

The X algorithm is now a single Grok-powered transformer that reads full text and video of every post. It makes roughly 5 billion ranking decisions per day. 

Published weights (relative to a like = 1×):

Action Weight
Reply (author responds) ~150×
Reply ~27×
Repost ~20×
Profile click ~12×
Link click ~11×
Bookmark ~10×
Like 1× (baseline)

Critical for sports content: Because Grok reads meaning, low-effort engagement bait and keyword stuffing work worse than before. Genuinely useful or interesting posts surface more reliably even from small accounts. The out-of-network pool is where growth lives.

1. GAP AUDIT REPORT

1.1 THE COLD-START CONTRADICTION — RESOLVED

Phase III said: No cold-start boost exists in the X code.
Phase III was WRONG. The xai-org/x-algorithm repository README explicitly lists a "New-Author Boost" in the scoring adjustments: "posts from authors whose impressions are below a threshold are lifted toward a target position."

What the code actually does (VERIFIED from primary source):

The new-author boost operates in RankingScorer alongside two other adjustments:

1. Author Diversity: Each post after an author's first is multiplied by a decaying factor, down to a floor. This prevents any single account from dominating a user's feed.
2. Out-of-Network Discount: Posts from accounts the viewer does not follow are multiplied by a factor below 1. Replies and reposts from followed accounts are also discounted.
3. New-Author Boost: Posts from authors whose impressions are below a threshold are lifted toward a target position.

How to exploit it (operator's action):

The boost is triggered by low impression count, not account age. A new account with few total impressions will have its posts lifted. The mechanism is a compensatory boost, not a "red carpet." It gives your content a fighting chance in the ranking, not a guarantee of distribution. To maximize the window:

· Post consistently from the start to build impression history — once you cross the threshold, the boost disappears.
· The boost does not override engagement quality. A weak post will still be filtered by low predicted engagement probabilities.
· The Author Diversity Scorer means posting multiple times in quick succession dilutes your reach per post. The boost does not protect against this.

Verdict: Phase III was correct that no "artificial boost" exists in the sense of a guaranteed distribution multiplier. But Phase III was WRONG to say no cold-start mechanism exists at all. The New-Author Boost is real, it is in the primary source, and it is compensatory rather than promotional.

1.2 THE FREQUENCY CONTRADICTION — RESOLVED

Phase III said: Post 3–5×/day on X. This contradicts Phase III's own findings.

The correct answer: 1–2×/day on X, 2–3×/day on TikTok, 1–2×/day on YouTube Shorts, 1–2×/day on Instagram Reels.

Why 3–5×/day on X is wrong:

The Author Diversity Scorer explicitly attenuates reach when the same account appears too frequently in a user's feed over a short window. The SocialPilot analysis states: "Creator diversity cap, a per-creator daily limit on how many posts of yours appear in any single follower's For You feed. Posting frequently doesn't increase your reach; it dilutes it across fewer viewers per post."

The mechanism is simple: if you post 5 times in a day, each post competes with the others for the same limited slots in your followers' feeds. The diversity scorer multiplies each post after the first by a decaying factor. You are not multiplying your reach — you are dividing it.

Optimal cadence per platform (VERIFIED from algorithm mechanics):

Platform Optimal posts/day Mechanism
X 1–2 Author Diversity Scorer; diversity cap per-creator
TikTok 2–3 Follower-first testing; each video gets a fresh test pool
YouTube Shorts 1–2 Shorts shelf; viewer satisfaction signals accumulate per video
Instagram Reels 1–2 Share-via-DM signals; originality scoring rewards fewer, better posts

What to do instead of posting more: Reply-chaining. Post once, then reply to your own post with additional analysis. The reply weight (27.0×) is the highest signal in the algorithm. You get the engagement benefit of a second post without triggering the diversity penalty.

1.7 THE TEXAS PROBLEM — RESOLVED

Phase III's betting-affiliate math was wrong for a Texas-heavy audience.

DraftKings Sportsbook Affiliates does not accept players from Texas, Florida, Nevada, Utah, California, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Georgia, Alabama, and other states. FanDuel Sportsbook does not accept players from Texas, Alaska, Florida, and other states.

What this means: If your audience is Texas-heavy, DraftKings and FanDuel affiliate links will convert at near-zero for Texas users. You will be paid only on players from states where the sportsbook operates.

Which affiliate programs accept Texas traffic and pay:

Program Texas traffic What they offer
DraftKings Predictions Yes (available in TX) Prediction markets, not sportsbook. Different affiliate program.
Kalshi Yes Prediction market. Affiliate program exists.
Polymarket Restricted (US) Not viable for US traffic.
DFS (DraftKings/FanDuel) Yes (if legal in TX) Daily fantasy sports may be legal in Texas. Check current status.
Sports betting affiliates No (TX excluded) DraftKings, FanDuel sportsbook affiliates will not pay on TX players.

Revised affiliate revenue math for Texas-heavy audience:

If 60% of your audience is in Texas, your effective conversion rate for sportsbook affiliates drops by ~60%. A 10K-follower account with 2% overall conversion to FTD becomes 0.8% effective conversion for Texas-heavy traffic. At $200 CPA, that is $160/year per 10K followers — essentially zero.

Strategic pivot: For a Texas-heavy audience, the viable monetization is prediction markets (Kalshi), DFS (if legal in Texas), or non-gambling revenue streams (sponsorships, merch, YouTube Shorts monetization).

4. INTEGRATION BLUEPRINTS (TOP 5)

Blueprint 1: yt-dlp + NFL+ → Footage on Disk

Goal: Download full game replay from NFL+ in under 60 seconds.

Step 1: Subscribe to NFL+ ($9.99/month). Log in via browser.

Step 2: Install yt-dlp:

```
pip install -U yt-dlp
```

Step 3: Download using cookies from browser:

```
yt-dlp --cookies-from-browser chrome --extractor-args "nflplusreplay:type=condensed_game" <game_url>
```

Step 4: Verify output:

```
ffprobe output.mp4
```

Fallback: If NFL+ is not viable, purchase a residential proxy ($5–15/GB) and use:

```
yt-dlp --proxy socks5://user:pass@proxy:port <nfl.com_url>
```

Blueprint 2: OBS + satoshate/obs_replay_script → Instant Capture

Goal: Capture the last 30 seconds of broadcast with one hotkey.

Step 1: Install OBS Studio. Configure replay buffer (Settings → Output → Replay Buffer → 30 seconds).

Step 2: Download script.py from satoshate/obs_replay_script. Add to OBS via Tools → Scripts.

Step 3: Assign hotkey: Settings → Hotkeys → "Save and restart replay buffer" → F9.

Step 4: During game, press F9 after a big play. Output goes to configured folder.

Blueprint 3: AutoSubZ → Captions

Goal: Auto-generate captions for a clip in under 30 seconds.

Step 1: Install:

```
pip install git+https://github.com/zaltinsoy/AutoSubZ.git
```

Step 2: Run:

```
auto_subtitle clip.mp4 -o subtitled/ --model medium
```

Step 3: Review and correct sports terms. Export burned-in captions:

```
ffmpeg -i subtitled/clip.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subtitled/clip.srt" clip_captioned.mp4
```

Blueprint 4: BrightBean Studio → Multi-Platform Publish

Goal: Publish one video to X, TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram from one dashboard.

Step 1: Deploy BrightBean Studio:

```
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 brightbeanxyz/brightbean-studio
```

Step 2: Connect platform accounts via OAuth (X, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram).

Step 3: Upload video, customize per-platform caption and hashtags, schedule or publish immediately.

Step 4: Monitor analytics in the unified dashboard.

Blueprint 5: nflverse-pbp + Tank01 → Play Detection

Goal: Detect a big play within 10 seconds of it happening.

Step 1: Subscribe to Tank01 NFL API (free tier: 1,000 requests/month).

Step 2: Poll /getNFLGameInfo every 10 seconds during games.

Step 3: When a play matches criteria (touchdown, turnover, 20+ yard gain), trigger OBS replay save via WebSocket API.

Step 4: Log play to PostgreSQL for later content generation (Lane 6).

SECTION 1 — VIRAL MECHANICS: HOW SPORTS CLIPS ACTUALLY SPREAD

1.1 The Four-Filter Model for Viral Clips

Every viral clip passes through four filters. If any filter fails, the clip dies. VERIFIED (GEN, June 2026) 

Filter Question Failure Mode
Hook Would someone stop scrolling in the first 1–2 seconds? Weak opening = algorithmic death
Context Can the viewer understand the moment quickly? Confusion = swipe away
Payoff Is there a clear reason to keep watching or share? No payoff = no completion
Repeatability Can this format be reused without feeling copied? One-off = no sustainable growth

1.2 The Six Content Types That Consistently Go Viral

VERIFIED (GEN, June 2026) 

1. Extreme or unexpected reactions — Human faces registering genuine surprise, disgust, laughter, or disbelief. Mirror neurons fire; the viewer feels what the subject feels. IShowSpeed built a global audience on this. Sports application: sideline reactions, fan reactions, player mic'd-up moments.
2. High-stakes or conflict moments from livestreams — Unscripted content where the outcome is uncertain for at least 10 seconds. Sports application: live game moments, clutch plays, controversial calls.
3. Comedy with clear punchline structure — The punchline must land before the viewer can scroll. Sports application: funny player interactions, meme-worthy moments.
4. Emotional peaks from live events — Sports is inherently emotional. The key is capturing the peak, not the entire event. Sports application: game-winning moments, player celebrations, post-game interviews.
5. Educational explainers with a twist — "Here's what you missed" or "Here's why that happened." Sports application: telestrated breakdowns, rules explanations, strategy analysis.
6. Before/after transformations — The highest watch-through rate of all hook types (85%). Sports application: pre-game prediction → post-game result, player before/after, season trajectory.

1.4 Platform-Specific Viral Thresholds (2026)

TikTok: Completion rate carries 40–50% of the algorithm's weight. The bar for viral pushes is now ~70% completion, up from ~50% in 2024. Reposts weigh ~10× more than likes. Saves weigh ~5× more. Follower count is NOT a ranking factor. 

YouTube Shorts: Viewer satisfaction has replaced watch time as the primary ranking signal. Surveys, repeat views, and shares now outweigh raw duration. The platform frames it as "satisfaction, not raw watch time." Swipe-away is a clean negative signal. 

Instagram Reels: DM sends are the strongest signal for showing a post to non-followers. Saves and shares now carry 3–5× the algorithmic weight of likes. The first 2–3 seconds are critical. 

X: Replies outweigh likes by approximately 27×. A reply the author answers can be worth ~150×. External links are throttled to near-zero for non-Premium accounts. Native video performs best, especially under 2:20. 

SECTION 2 — ALGORITHM DEEP DIVE PER PLATFORM

2.1 TikTok: The 10-Day Test

Every video earns 96% of its views in the first 10 days. The algorithm tests in waves: first your followers, then cold audiences in pools of 200–500, then wider. Pass the test (completion, reposts, saves), and you get the next wave. Fail, and distribution fades. 

Ranking factors by weight:

Factor Weight How to optimize
Completion rate 40–50% Keep videos short; hook in first 1s; loop-friendly endings
Reposts ~10× a like Create shareable, DM-worthy moments
Saves ~5× a like Reference content: stats, rankings, analysis
Likes Baseline (weakest) Do not optimize for likes
Follower-first testing Gatekeeper Build an engaged small following before scaling

Critical insight: A "dead" or botted audience now actively sinks new videos because the algorithm tests with followers first. 

2.2 YouTube Shorts: Satisfaction Over Duration

The 2026 update replaced watch time with viewer satisfaction. The platform pipes post-view survey results into ranking. On Shorts, a swipe-away is a clean negative signal. 

Key mechanic: YouTube rebuilt large parts of recommendation in 2026. Well-optimized Shorts can now appear directly in regular search results and the Home feed alongside long-form videos when relevant. 

What this means for sports content: Shorts are no longer a separate island. A telestrated breakdown Short can surface in search results for "how to read cover 2." SEO-optimized titles and descriptions matter more than they did in 2024.

2.3 Instagram Reels: The Send Economy

Instagram ranks follower engagement and non-follower reach separately. A post with 200 likes and 2 sends stays home; a post with 40 likes and 30 sends travels. 

The four signals that earn non-follower reach:

1. Sends (DM shares) — Strongest signal. Create something one specific person would forward to one specific friend.
2. Saves — A save means the viewer intends to come back. Reference content earns saves.
3. Watch time — For Reels, the share of the video watched and rewatched decides whether it's shown to the next batch.
4. Profile visits and follows — A post that makes people open your profile is treated as worth showing to similar people.

2.4 X: The Conversation Engine

The X algorithm is now a single Grok-powered transformer that reads full text and video of every post. It makes roughly 5 billion ranking decisions per day. 

Published weights (relative to a like = 1×):

Action Weight
Reply (author responds) ~150×
Reply ~27×
Repost ~20×
Profile click ~12×
Link click ~11×
Bookmark ~10×
Like 1× (baseline)

Critical for sports content: Because Grok reads meaning, low-effort engagement bait and keyword stuffing work worse than before. Genuinely useful or interesting posts surface more reliably even from small accounts. The out-of-network pool is where growth lives.

8.1 The Storyline Engine

Every sports season is a narrative arc. The storyline engine maps:

Week Narrative Beat Content Format
1–4 "Who are the contenders?" Power rankings, early picks

8.2 The Hook-to-Payoff Chain

Every video must complete this chain in under 30 seconds:

1. Hook (0–2s): Visual break, provocative statement, or before/after reveal
2. Context (2–5s): What are we looking at? Why does it matter?
3. Evidence (5–20s): Telestrated breakdown, stat overlay, or clip sequence
4. Payoff (20–28s): The insight, the receipt, the lesson
5. Loop (28–30s): Seamless return to start or clear end card

8.3 The Review & Grading Rubric

Every video gets scored before publish:

Dimension Weight Criteria
Hook strength 25% Would a stranger stop scrolling?
Telestration accuracy 20% Are the arrows/circles correct?
Caption sync 15% Are captions synced to voiceover?
Voiceover quality 15% Is the commentary clear and on-brand?
Payoff clarity 15% Is there a clear reason to share?
Loop mechanics 10% Does it end cleanly?

Serial review process: Videos scoring below 70% go back to edit. Videos scoring 70–85% publish on schedule. Videos scoring 85%+ get boosted distribution (post at peak times, cross-post to all platforms).

Week 1 answered a few backfield questions and created about nine new ones. Percentages assume a $100 season budget, because pretending your FAAB is unlimited is how benches get ugly.
1. Kyle Monangai, RB, Chicago Bears
Monangai turned 10 carries into 100 yards and a touchdown, and the score came on a 61-yard run that likely cost somebody their waiver priority. Ben Johnson praised him after the game, which is the closest thing to a public commitment a head coach offers in September. He is the true 1B to D'Andre Swift in an elite run game, and the knee scare from early camp is behind him. Bid 25 to 30 percent. He is the one back here whose role grows even if nobody gets hurt.
2. Blake Corum, RB, Los Angeles Rams
The 10 carries for 54 yards will not win you a week on their own, but the near 50/50 split with Kyren Williams is real. Williams still owns third downs and the goal line, though, and those are the snaps that pay in fantasy. That leaves Corum an elite handcuff with fringe flex value in the right matchup rather than a starter. Bid 10 to 15 percent, and push toward 20 if Williams is already on your roster.
3. Emmett Johnson, RB, Kansas City Chiefs
The passing-down work is the tell: two catches for 44 yards next to eight carries for 24. Johnson is the clear RB2 behind Kenneth Walker III, and Kansas City shows no interest in turning that into a committee. Premium handcuff stash, zero standalone value while Walker is healthy, which makes him the most annoying kind of player to hold. 4. Kaelon Black, RB, San Francisco 49ers
Black out-carried Christian McCaffrey 14 to 10, the kind of line that gets a backup rostered everywhere by Wednesday. He finished with 65 yards on the ground plus one catch for five, and the explanation is cramps plus planned workload management, a polite way of saying San Francisco would like McCaffrey upright in December. Black is a designed 1B rather than a gadget, and his value is tied entirely to the health of the man in front of him. Bid 10 to 15 percent if you do not roster McCaffrey, and closer to 20 if you do.

**The three sauces (one base, three heats)**

Blend into a base: 1 small red onion, 8 garlic cloves, 1 red bell pepper, 1/3 cup white vinegar, 1/4 cup neutral oil, 1 tbsp smoked paprika, 2 tsp oregano, 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp sugar, 2 bay leaves. Simmer 15–20 minutes, fish out the bay, blend smooth, then stir in the zest and juice of 2 lemons (lemon goes in after cooking or it turns bitter). This is your mild foundation.

- **Mild:** 2–3 bird's eye chilies, simmer 5 min
- **Hot:** 6–8 bird's eye chilies, simmer 10 min
- **Extra hot:** 12–15 bird's eye chilies + 1 habanero, seeds in, simmer 10 min

Blend each smooth. Taste and adjust salt or lemon. They keep 2–3 weeks refrigerated and get better after a day.

Key grocery note: fresh "Thai chilies" at HEB are African bird's eye chilies, same pepper. Wear gloves on the extra hot batch.

**The rice**

Sauté diced onion, garlic, and half a red bell pepper; bloom 1 tsp turmeric (that's what makes it yellow), 1/2 tsp smoked paprika, 1/2 tsp cumin, and a spoon of your mild sauce; stir in 1 cup rinsed basmati; add 2 cups chicken stock; simmer covered 12–15 minutes; toss in some frozen peas at the end.

    case pending, won, lost, push, void
    var id: String { rawValue }

    var label: String {
        switch self {
        case .pending: "Pending"; case .won: "Won"
        case .lost: "Lost";       case .push: "Push"
        case .void: "Void"
        }
    }

struct UserBet: Identifiable, Codable, Hashable {
    var id: UUID = UUID()
    var eventName: String
    var selection: String
    var odds: Int
    var stake: Double
    var sportsbook: String
    var placedAt: Date
    var status: BetStatus
    var notes: String = ""
    var linkedPickID: String? = nil

    /// Total returned including stake on a win; stake on push/void.
    func payout(unitSize: Double) -> Double {
        switch status {
        case .won:
            return odds > 0
                ? stake * (1 + Double(odds) / 100)
                : stake * (1 + 100 / Double(-odds))
        case .push, .void: return stake
        case .lost: return 0
        case .pending: return 0
        }
    }

    func profit(unitSize: Double) -> Double {
        switch status {
        case .won:  return payout(unitSize: unitSize) - stake
        case .lost: return -stake
        case .push, .void, .pending: return 0
        }
    }
} import Foundation

enum APIError: LocalizedError {
    case invalidURL
    case unauthorized
    case notFound
    case rateLimited
    case server(status: Int, message: String?)
    case decoding(Error)
    case transport(Error)
    case offline

    var errorDescription: String? {
        switch self {
        case .invalidURL:               "That request couldn't be built."
        case .unauthorized:             "Your session expired. Please sign in again."
        case .notFound:                 "We couldn't find what you were looking for."

        case .server(let s, let m):     m ?? "Server error (\(s))."
        case .decoding:                 "We got an unexpected response from the server."
        case .transport(let e):         (e as NSError).localizedDescription
        case .offline:                  "You appear to be offline."
        }
    }

    var isRetryable: Bool {
        switch self {
        case .rateLimited, .server, .transport, .offline: true
