# EXAM — 17 IG finds through the GSE + revenue lenses (2026-09-30)

Garrett's order: look at all of them "in exam," from GSE and revenue, outside the box, dynamically. This is that.

## The scorecard

| # | Find | GSE value | Revenue value | Verdict |
|---|------|-----------|---------------|---------|
| 1 | Freebuff ($0 coding agent) | Medium — $0 build capacity for engine tooling | High — $0 build capacity for client work, video factory, everything | ADOPT. The fuel for max-autonomy mode. |
| 2 | Higgsfield heist pipeline | None directly — real-footage rule blocks it for sports | High — the method for the AI-content lane's top of funnel | ADAPT the method, never the content. Sports lane untouched. |
| 3 | GBP management ($500/mo retainers) | None | Highest near-term — recurring, tool-assisted fulfillment | The backend the whole funnel feeds. Claims unverified; mechanics sound. |
| 4 | CourtListener vetting app | Low | Medium — vet clients/partners; potential product | Build the internal version first. |
| 5 | Perchance free generators | Low | Low-medium — $0 thumbnails/mockups if quality passes | Test against the design bar before any customer sees it. |
| 6 | Claude+Quiver+Robinhood loop | None | Speculative — crowded copy-trading, thin edge | Paper trade only. Not a revenue plan today. |
| 7 | Kev (free Jev stand-in) | Medium — decisions layer for analysis agents | Medium — decisions layer for client/ops agents | Reopens the parked lane at $0. Garrett's call to reopen. |
| 8 | Scenario agent skills | Low-medium — thumbnails, video assets | High — agent-generated media with price-before-spend | The art department for the video factory. |
| 9 | coingecko-jev | None | Unverified claim; community builds real but thin | Watch, don't chase. |
| 10 | kem_glitch interface skins | Low | Medium — mission-control UI for the fleet | The pattern matters more than the repo. |
| 11 | TypeLLM (typed output) | Medium — structured engine data | High — structured everything: pipelines, QC, extraction | Invisible plumbing that makes the machine reliable. |
| 12 | EgoExoMoCap | None | Low — hardware-gated, research-grade | Park until hardware exists. |
| 13 | RelateAnything | HIGH — film-pipeline component (play segmentation, moment search) | Low-medium — scene analysis for content | The single best sports find of the night. Gates still stand. |
| 14 | FreeMoCap | Low for GSE | Medium — cheap mocap for AI-character content | The practical mocap path. <$100. |
| 15 | OpenMuse | Low | Medium — persistent phone-side agent | Alpha. Evaluate, don't depend. |
| 16 | xvr | None | None | Filed, not a priority. |
| 17 | InstantHMR | Low-medium — pose data from stills | Medium — pose/mesh from any phone photo | Most accessible mocap tier. Free, on-device. |

## The compounds — where 1+1=5

These are the real finds. Individually they're tools; combined they're machines.

**Compound A — the $0 autonomous stack.** Freebuff (execution) + Kev (judgment) + TypeLLM (data shape) + OpenMuse (persistence). Four layers, zero dollars. A coding agent that builds for free, a decision model that judges for free, typed outputs that keep every step structured and auditable, and a persistent agent that keeps working after the phone closes. This is the first time the "maximum autonomy" directive has had a $0 bill of materials. Run the video factory on this stack and the factory's marginal cost is electricity.

**Compound B — the video factory's full production chain.** Higgsfield method (what goes viral + lookalike distribution) + Scenario skills (agent-generated media, price-transparent) + FreeMoCap/InstantHMR (real human motion and poses) + Perchance (free thumbnails) + RelateAnything (scene understanding). Every stage of "make tons of high quality videos" is covered by something found tonight. The factory isn't a wish anymore — it's a parts list.

**Compound C — the revenue flywheel.** Viral AI-tool videos (top of funnel, Compound B) → Loom-style audit outreach (the GBP playbook's best mechanic) → Kit sites $350 (entry) → GBP retainers ~$500/mo (recurring core) → AI Receptionist $49/mo (attach). Every video is a prospecting asset; every client funds more videos. The funnel Garrett already built finally has its top.

**Compound D — the QC layer.** TypeLLM + Kev turns every agent decision into a typed, logged, auditable verdict. Motif QC-gates proofs on the agent bus today by hand; this is the path to the bus gating itself. Decisions with calibrated probabilities instead of vibes.

**Compound E — the mission-control UI.** kem_glitch's pattern (headless agents stream events → skin an interface on top) + OpenMuse (persistent agent with a phone app) + Garrett's Unseen-Studio design bar. One dashboard to watch the whole fleet. This is leverage on leverage: the machine, visible.

## Outside the box

- **RelateAnything as a viral-mining engine.** The Higgsfield playbook says "mine the top 100 viral posts" with eyeballs. Point RelateAnything at them instead: what object relationships recur in viral frames? That's computer-vision market research — find the visual grammar of virality, then generate into it with Scenario. Nobody in the reel comments is doing this.
- **CourtListener as a product, not just a tool.** "Know who you're doing business with" is sellable to the same local businesses buying GBP management. Due-diligence reports as a $99 one-time or an upsell. And defensively: vet every guru, course seller, and counterparty before Garrett spends a minute on them — including the GBP course sellers whose income claims didn't verify.
- **The heist pipeline's transferable half.** The sports lane can't touch the remake half (real-footage rule). But the *distribution* half — commenter analysis → lookalike audiences → serving content back to the lookalikes — is platform mechanics, not content theft. That half ports cleanly to GSE's legitimate clips.
- **FreeMoCap for client work, not just content.** Local businesses pay for product demos and spokesperson videos. A $100 webcam rig producing mocap-driven spokesperson content is a service with real margin inside the GBP/Kit stack.
- **InstantHMR for Marketplace.** Pose-accurate human meshes from a phone photo — stage product photos (cards, collectibles, signage mockups) with real human scale reference. Small, but it's free.
- **Scenario's price-before-spend as doctrine.** The single most important mechanic in tonight's haul isn't a tool, it's a policy: no agent spends anything without stating the price first. That should govern every agent in the fleet, not just media generation.

## Dynamic sequences — what unlocks what

**Sequence 1 (revenue, weeks):** Stand up the $0 stack (Compound A) → video factory produces AI-tool demos daily (Compound B) → each video ends in the Loom-audit offer → Kit sites → GBP retainers (Compound C). The flywheel funds itself from the first $350.

**Sequence 2 (GSE, gated):** Evaluate RelateAnything against real footage the moment legitimate sourcing clears → play-segmentation prototype → semantic moment search → better analysis → traffic → 1,000 visitors → product work unlocks. The gates don't move; the component waits ready.

**Sequence 3 (leverage, ongoing):** Mission-control UI (Compound E) → the fleet becomes visible → Garrett runs the operation from his phone → OpenMuse-style persistence means it runs while he sleeps. The operation stops being a set of chats and becomes a machine with a dashboard.

## What dies

- xvr: no lane. Filed, forgotten.
- coingecko-jev's official-repo claim: unverified. The community builds are real but thin-edge. Watch only.
- EgoExoMoCap: parked until smart-glasses hardware exists. FreeMoCap and InstantHMR cover the need cheaper.
- The Quiver/Robinhood loop as revenue: crowded, thin edge, real money. Paper trade or nothing.
- GBP income claims ($12.9k/mo, 6 months, 39 families): unverified. The mechanics are adopted; the numbers are not repeated.
- Higgsfield's 100% cashback: expired tonight. The method survives; the subsidy doesn't.

## The one-line exam result

Tonight's haul contains a $0 autonomous agent stack, a complete video-factory parts list, the clearest sports component found in weeks (RelateAnything), and a revenue flywheel whose top of funnel finally exists. The exam says: build the stack, feed the flywheel, evaluate RelateAnything the day footage clears.

title: EYI: workspace/goals/autonomous-revenue-engine/files/EXAM-2026-09-30-morning-deep-dive.md
body:
# Deep re-examination — the morning's haul (findings 26–35)
Date: 2026-09-30. Second pass over everything Garrett sent this morning, slower and more
introspective than the first filing. The question is not "what is this" but "where does it
fit, what does it combine with, and what am I not seeing."

Two carousel reads are still in flight (@aitechorigin's open-source-tools roundup,
@parasmadan.in's OpenAI Dev Day 2026 recap) and are NOT in this pass — they get folded in
when they land.

---

## Per-finding deep reads

### 26. Five practical AI/ML projects — infrastructure thinking disguised as tutorials
First verdict was "beginner, low priority." On reflection that's lazy. The tutorials are
beginner; the architectures are not. Two carry real weight:

- **RAG-over-PDFs** is the seed of a queryable layer over the intelligence corpus itself.
  Right now 35 findings live as markdown. A RAG layer turns them into something askable:
  "what did we learn about free video tooling?" That is how the corpus compounds instead
  of just accumulating.
- **XGBoost + SHAP** is the more important one. GSE's hard doctrine: projections public,
  methodology private. SHAP-style explainability is the mechanism that satisfies both —
  explain WHY a pick was made (feature contributions) without revealing the model. The
  public/private fence has been a constraint; explainability turns it into a feature.
  "Here's what drove this pick" is content. It is also trust: followers see the work
  without seeing the recipe.

Second-order: churn prediction maps weakly to subscriber churn if GSE ever has
subscribers; the recommender maps weakly to content recommendation. Both are reaches.
The honest yield is RAG + explainability. Neither needs new tooling — both are
architecture, applicable with what exists.

### 27. "Secret hidden AI websites" — steal the format, not the tools
The tools were the decoy. The finding is the GENRE: "secret tools" carousels are a
distribution format that drives saves, and saves are the highest-intent Instagram
interaction. For GSE's own content, the "secret" framing is stealable — "the metrics
nobody talks about," etc. — without touching the tools themselves.

The ZSKY wordmark lie is the more valuable data point: these aggregator accounts do not
verify. Base rate of false claims in the carousel genre is high. Our verification habit
is the edge; this finding justifies keeping it expensive. Every future carousel claim
starts guilty until verified.

Dynamic note: these accounts are themselves a distribution vector. If GSE ever wants
tool awareness seeded (motion-skills, the agency stack), the "secret tools" accounts are
the channel, not the source.

### 28. .gov backlinks — a valuable negative result
The creator admitted registration does not guarantee a backlink, indexing, or ranking.
That kills a whole category of SEO busywork before it starts — a negative result is a
result. The transferable concept is GEO/AEO: the modern backlink game is being cited by
AI answers. The question for GSE is not "who links to us" but "when someone asks an AI
about NFL predictions, do we surface?" The intelligence corpus, the public projections,
the explained picks — that is cite-worthy material. Park stands; the reframe is the yield.

### 29. Google Trends drill — a timing weapon, and half a pipeline
The mechanic (category → rising → subtopic → scheduled content) is content arbitrage:
publish into rising interest before it peaks. But Trends is lagging — it shows what is
already rising. The real edge is predicting the rise, which is the same muscle as GSE's
engine applied to a different domain.

The dynamic read: this is HALF of a machine. The other half arrived this morning as
finding 33. Trends drill detects the topic; motion-skills' data-animation and explainer
packs generate the video; publish. Detect → generate → publish, weekly cycle. Neither
finding is a machine alone. Together they are the closest thing to one in the morning's
haul.

### 30. Meta SAM 3D Body — the tech is not the constraint
Single-image 3D mesh recovery from broadcast frames is the bridge from 2D video to 3D
analytics: pose, body orientation, separation at the catch point. The license split
(Apache code, SAM-licensed weights) is the silent-killer pattern — commercial use dies
in the weights license, not the code license. Always read both.

The dynamic combination: SAM 3D Body extracts meshes from real frames; synthetic
Blender scenes (finding 22's method) generate labeled meshes; the two validate each
other. Real → mesh → synthetic → train → real. A closed loop.

The introspective correction: the tech excitement must not reorder the constraints.
The binding constraints are patent families and footage legality, not mesh quality.
A better model does not clear a single legal gate. Tech second, gates first.

### 31. The agency stack — the pattern is the product
The five tools are not the insight. The PATTERN is: find → orchestrate → track →
respond → close, as a closed loop at $0. That is the Kit lane's missing machine — Kit
outreach is currently manual. But "free" here is the puppy problem: self-hosting five
services is operational load that costs Garrett's scarcest resource (his time/attention,
and ours).

The sharper play is cherry-picking, not adopting: Twenty (CRM) + Activepieces
(orchestration) as the core; Documenso only when a contract actually needs signing;
Firecrawl only where audit personalization earns its keep. Adopt the loop, not the stack.

What would change the assessment: license verification on Twenty, Chatwoot,
Activepieces. If any of the "clean" three turns out copyleft, the cherry-picked subset
collapses and the whole thing reprices.

### 32. Jev testimonial — parking is a decision
No new tool; the lane stays dark at his word. The discipline being tested: Jev content
will keep arriving, each piece making the parked lane look more alive. FOMO is not a
reopening gate. If the lane ever reopens, the first test is not the tool — it is whether
pattern extraction beats manual review on a timed trial. Until then: dark.

### 33. motion-skills — the most important MECHANIC of the morning
The 54 skills matter less than the deliver-and-verify loop: render a frame, screenshot
it, check it. The agent inspects its own output instead of hoping. That is a general
pattern, not a video pattern. Apply it everywhere agents produce artifacts: code
(run → observe → check), outreach drafts (render preview → check), stat cards, reports.
"Show your work" made mechanical.

The binding constraint is the Unseen bar. The test is not "does it render" — it is
"does it clear the bar." These packs can produce competent motion graphics; competent
is the enemy. One pack, one render, judged against the bar, or the verdict means nothing.

Dynamic: this is the generation half of finding 29's pipeline. Trends → topic →
data-animation/explainer pack → publish.

### 34. QuantMuse — a "looks relevant, isn't" finding
Quant finance and sports prediction share math vocabulary and different data-generating
processes. Factor-model language (momentum, value, quality, volatility) maps loosely
onto sports factors and then breaks — markets mean-revert differently than matchups do.
The discipline is recognizing domain-transfer limits before investing.

The durable signal: 2,952 stars, dead for 14 months. Stars are a lagging indicator of
aliveness. Check push dates on everything, forever.

### 35. Devin Desktop — the platform-risk case study
The Windsurf saga (OpenAI deal collapses → Google acquihires the team → Cognition buys
the remainder) is why you do not build load-bearing workflow on someone else's IDE: the
ground moves. The interesting bit is not the product — it is ACP, the Agent Client
Protocol. If ACP standardizes, agents become composable across surfaces and the fleet
gets Paperclip (open, $0) plus ACP-compatible agents without the $20/month. Watch the
protocol, not the product. And the reel is marketing, not a review — "best IDE" is
bought or farmed, discounted accordingly.

---

## Cross-cutting dynamic plays (the morning as a system, not a list)

**Play A — the rapid-response content pipeline.** Finding 29 (detect rising topics) +
finding 33 (generate explainers/data animations via skill packs) + publish. Weekly
cycle, testable in one week: run the Trends drill Monday, generate one explainer,
measure. This is the only closed-loop machine the morning produced.

**Play B — the 3D analytics loop.** Finding 30 (SAM 3D Body meshes from real frames) +
finding 22's synthetic method (Blender scenes, RelateAnything patterns) validating each
other. Still behind the patent and footage gates — the loop is designed, not cleared.

**Play C — the Kit acquisition machine.** Finding 31's loop (find → orchestrate →
track → respond → close), cherry-picked: Twenty + Activepieces core, the rest on demand.
This is Kit's missing automation. License verification is the gating work.

**Play D — explainability as the public/private fence.** Finding 26's SHAP pattern:
explain picks publicly (feature contributions as content and trust) without revealing
methodology. Turns the hardest doctrine constraint into a content format.

**Play E — the verify loop as universal QC.** Finding 33's render → screenshot → check,
generalized to all agent artifacts. This is a doctrine candidate: no agent output ships
without a self-inspection step.

---

## Introspection — what could I be getting wrong

- **Carousel base rate.** The genre lies (ZSKY wordmark). Our verification habit is
  correct and must stay expensive. Never let a morning of mostly-verified findings
  lower the guard.
- **Star-count bias.** Stars measure past attention, not present aliveness. Push dates
  are the vital sign.
- **Tech excitement vs. binding constraints.** SAM 3D Body does not outrank the patent
  and footage gates. Whenever a finding is exciting, ask: what is the actual binding
  constraint, and did this move it?
- **Parked-lane FOMO.** Jev content will keep arriving. Parking is a decision; only
  Garrett reopens.
- **The morning's real yield is patterns, not tools.** Verify-loops, rapid-response
  pipelines, explainability-as-fence, cherry-picked stacks. Tools rot; patterns compound.
- **What I have not tested.** None of the five plays has been run. Every verdict above
  the "filed" level needs a test with a pass/fail gate, or it is just a well-written
  opinion. The next step for each play is named in its reopening gate, not in more analysis.

## Addendum — finding 37: @aitechorigin open-source tools carousel (landed after the first pass)

All 10 slides read; 9 repos verified via GitHub API. Cover claims "10 repos," shows 9 —
engagement-bait inflation. The carousel's OpenChatCut path 404s; the real repo is
0xsline/OpenChatCut — second data point that big accounts don't verify paths.

**The deep read:** this carousel is the "$0-stack genre," and the corpus has now
converged: multiple candidates per slot (scraping: maxun vs Firecrawl; scheduling:
mixpost vs shoutrrr; editing: OpenChatCut; builders: webstudio vs plasmic). The phase
shifts from collecting candidates to running bake-offs per slot. More lists don't help;
one test per slot does.

The sleeper is OpenWhispr (MIT, 8.9k stars, active): voice-to-text that serves Garrett
directly. His dictation is garbled; the founder is the bottleneck; personal-leverage
tools outrank business tools here. This is the highest personal-ROI item in the carousel.

License map: maxun AGPL, webstudio AGPL, OpenChatCut AGPL — the no-code/agent-friendly
slots all carry copyleft. The MIT-clean subset (OpenWhispr, plasmic, mixpost, shoutrrr)
is where adoption lives; AGPL stays learn-don't-integrate.

Revised verdict: QUEUE per-slot bake-offs (scraping, scheduling, editing); QUEUE
OpenWhispr as a personal-workflow test. mixpost/shoutrrr scoped to scheduling/drafting
only — never autonomous publishing, per the approval doctrine.

---

## Addendum — finding 36: OpenAI Dev Day 2026 (landed after the first pass)

The @parasmadan.in carousel read landed and its claims verified against news coverage.
Folded into the pass as promised.

**The deep read:** Dots is the industry converging on Garrett's architecture — persistent
agents with goals, app connections, and permission boundaries are exactly what his crons,
agent bus, and subagents already do. Convergence validates the direction; it does not
require adopting the product (paid tiers only, and his fleet is $0 by doctrine).

The genuine steal is the permission-boundary MODEL: three explicit tiers — acts alone /
needs approval / must never do. His fleet currently runs on looser conventions. Making
those tiers explicit in the agent-bus doctrine is free and sharpens every delegation.

GPT-6.1 Sol's pricing ($2/$10 per M, 95% cached-input discount) sets the number to beat:
any video-factory or agent-pipeline generation cost gets measured against ~$2/M input.
Not a buy — a benchmark.

The Decisions API ("Jev competitor" per one outlet) is a data point for the parked Jev
lane: the decision-layer space is commoditizing. If the lane ever reopens, the build-vs-
buy math has shifted. It does not reopen the lane.

Revised verdict: QUEUE the permission-tier doctrine for the agent bus; WATCH Sol pricing
as the cost benchmark. The carousel's accuracy is a credibility point for @parasmadan.in
as a future source.

---

## Revised verdicts and reopening gates

| Finding | Revised verdict | Reopening gate |
|---|---|---|
| 26 (ML projects) | ADOPT the patterns (RAG corpus layer, SHAP-as-fence) | A RAG query demo over the corpus; one SHAP-style pick explanation |
| 27 (AI websites) | PARK (format steal noted) | — |
| 28 (.gov backlinks) | PARK (GEO/AEO reframe banked) | Evidence GSE is/ isn't AI-cited |
| 29 (Trends drill) | QUEUE as Play A's detection half | One weekly cycle run end-to-end |
| 30 (SAM 3D Body) | QUEUE (loop designed, gates stand) | Patent-family review + footage legality |
| 31 (agency stack) | QUEUE cherry-picked (Twenty + Activepieces) | License verification on the clean three |
| 32 (Jev) | PARKED — stays dark | Garrett's word only |
| 33 (motion-skills) | QUEUE, high priority | One pack rendered against the Unseen bar |
| 34 (QuantMuse) | PARK (learning ref only) | — |
| 35 (Devin Desktop) | PARK behind Paperclip; watch ACP | Paperclip evaluation completes |

- The honest math: +$3.6M on $399.3M volume ≈ **0.9% edge** — the signature of a capitalized high-frequency market-making operation, not a miracle compounder. Bot or human desk, the edge is micro, the volume is everything.
- Regulatory context (REPORTED, multiple outlets 2026-06): CFTC probing Polymarket after WSJ reported the company paid social-media creators to post videos of fake/simulated trades with exaggerated winnings, often undisclosed. - Assessment: more interesting than pure fabrication — the wallet is real money, real profit — but the "$1 Claude bot" narrative is the reel's invention. Transferable signal: high-volume micro-edge market-making works on prediction markets; the 0.9%-edge math is the honest version of the story. Sports-lane note: the claimed markets are sports (CBB/football/NBA) — adjacent to prediction-market analytics, not to the engine.
- Verdict: **PARK as a research thread** (reopening gate: a paper-trading market-making experiment with honest accounting, or on-chain evidence of the bot's actual strategy). - Source: https://instagram.com/p/Dd5TMGQIn7K/ (@choicooks / CHOICOOKS, 56,183 followers; video, 91 likes, 54 comments, posted 2026-09-29). Caption: "comment "CLASS" and ill send over the free training" — comments at 59% of likes, classic comment-gate signature.

Example: Dallas Wings vs Golden State Valkyries — $100 on Over 182.5 at -110 (Fliff) + $2 on Under 182.5 at +9900 (Kalshi) = $102 wager, "guaranteed" $88 or $98 profit regardless of outcome, called a 46.5% arbitrage. Claims a student made $90 in five minutes live. On-screen graphics show an interface labeled "Sweet Station" (unidentified) and define arbitrage.

The coexistence is CLAIMED — +9900 on Kalshi vs -110 on Fliff implies an enormous cross-platform mispricing; such gaps in illiquid markets close in seconds to arb bots, so the example reads as cherry-picked or staged. $30k/month CLAIMED/unverified; the student anecdote is CLAIMED hype. Fliff is a sweepstakes/social sportsbook (coin redemption, minimums, playthrough) — real-money execution is constrained. "Sweet Station" is unidentified. No repo, no code, nothing independently verifiable.
- Assessment: promo funnel for a free-training→likely-paid-course/Discord pipeline, not a tool. Transferable mechanic: cross-platform arb scanning between Kalshi's free API and sportsbook lines is a real idea and pairs with the trading handoff's items #6 (free Kalshi API) and #7 (Kalshi bot chassis) — but execution needs funded accounts on both sides, which the paper-trading-only boundary forbids.

- Source: https://instagram.com/p/DXcgx3cgNzK/ (@github_unpacked "Github Unpacked", 19,055 followers; video, posted 2026-04-22; 1,173 likes, 9 comments). Garrett sent 2026-09-30.

Good for backtests, market-efficiency studies, wallet-level analysis.

Connects to the verified free Polymarket API (item #6) — this is the historical-data side of that free feed.

## 69. Meta SAM 3 + Roboflow basketball tracking demo — open-vocabulary player tracking, real
- Source: https://instagram.com/p/DYkkCmcRN_t/ (@metav3rse, 1.55M followers, curator account; posted 2026-05-20, 5,666 likes, 61 comments; credit: Roboflow). Media-understanding narrative retrieved: live NBA playoff footage (Celtics home game), every player rendered as a color silhouette tracked frame-by-frame with a court-diagram trail map below; later frames add ID labels (#25 Bridges, #11 Brunson, #7 Brown, #42 Horford) plus team colors. - Verification: **SAM 3 VERIFIED real** — released November 19, 2025 per Meta/Roboflow/Wikipedia/arXiv 2511.16719. Promptable Concept Segmentation: text prompts ("player in white jersey") or exemplars drive detect+segment+track across images and video; open source under the custom SAM License (commercial OK, restrictions apply); ~848M params, checkpoints + inference/fine-tuning code released; free web playground on Roboflow.
- Honest caveats (third-party sports-tracking migration assessment, public GitHub doc): weights gated on HuggingFace (request-access lag); no official streaming API (community bridges exist); video latency scales with tracked-object count; SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex (~30fps on H100, 16 objects/forward pass) is the first config where a full 10-player scene is realistically live — that's H100/A100-class money. SAM doesn't know player vs ref vs bench and can't do team/jersey ID on its own; a classifier on mask crops still handles ID-swap arbitration.
- Assessment: this is the same lane as #50 (GPT-6 Astra jersey ID) — general VLMs reducing custom player-identification work. The transferable insight is the concept-prompt formulation: "player in white jersey" replaces custom detectors. But it does NOT clear the standing film-pipeline gates: (1) legitimate footage sourcing — the demo uses NBA playoff broadcast footage, rights unresolved; (2) the three-game hand-labeled validation set is still the measurement bar, and ID-swap rate/track continuity remain unmeasured; (3) patent-family/continuation review unaffected.
- Trading lens: not trading-related. No trading-handoff addition; that file stays 100% GSE-free.
- Verdict: **QUEUE** as a film-pipeline method reference. Reopening gate: run SAM 3 against the planned three-game hand-labeled validation set once legitimately-sourced footage exists — measure ID-swap rate and track continuity before any build commitment. **PARK** for trading.

The "100% hit rate" framing is the same unverified-accuracy theater as #55 (Airia) and #65 (JEV'S PICK). Not trading-related — no trading-handoff addition, that file stays GSE-free.

## 72. Tunde Alao tests "MirrorFish" (MiroFish) for content-virality prediction — same repo as #59, n=5 demo
- Source: https://instagram.com/p/Ddtt8NFCUSp/ (Tunde Alao, @itstundeanthony, 234,536 followers; "Fact or Hype?" series). Posted 2026-09-25, 2,196 likes, 562 comments. Caption is thin: comment-gated ("Comment "fish""), same gate as #59.

He clones the GitHub repo, runs it locally (UI in Chinese, switched to English), feeds it transcripts of 5 of his own videos, asks which will perform best. The tool builds a knowledge graph, simulates agents posting/commenting, and reports the "brag video" (Episode 14) as top — which matches his actual analytics (~900k views). The tool is almost certainly **666ghj/MiroFish from finding #59** — same Chinese UI, same agent-simulation design, same "comment 'fish'" gate. MiroFish: VERIFIED real, 75k stars, AGPL-3.0, active. The virality-prediction claim: CLAIMED — n=5, self-reported, retrodictive, no held-out test. Comment sentiment is mixed: token-cost questions, requests for more testing, plus scam warnings ("a guy trying to exploit the real project").
- Assessment: not trading-related (content-virality demo) — no trading-handoff addition; the file stays GSE-free. Revenue-adjacent as a tool reference: crowd-simulation for forecasting content performance is a real method worth testing on held-out data. The creator's own joke ("might kill my OpenAI credits") flags the cost problem: simulating hundreds of agents per prediction is expensive — token economics must be measured before any serious use. - Source: https://instagram.com/p/DbOLW3hFUL0/ (@thelocktalk | Jason Seo, 26,752 followers). Carousel posted 2026-07-25, 899 likes, 143 comments (~16% comment-to-like ratio = gate signature). Headline: "HOW TO TURN CHATGPT INTO A NRFI GENIUS."

- Assessment: this account is already in the people index — Garrett saves and transcribes these prompt carousels into the action board (9 gated prompts already awaiting his phone taps from the TD/HR and live-NFL sets). The three angles are legitimate handicapping questions (first-inning splits, situational rust, lineup-top danger) packaged as prompt engineering; no track record posted. QUEUE: transcribe the prompts into the action board like the prior sets; grade the three angles against actual NRFI outcomes as the reopening gate. **Not trading-related — no trading-handoff addition.**

## 75. @darshcoded "3 World Cup data science projects" — portfolio-idea reel, comment-gated resources
- Source: https://instagram.com/p/DXOFvkSjVVa/ (darsh / @darshcoded, 34,458 followers). Reel posted 2026-04-16, 24,735 likes, 5,757 comments (~23% comment-to-like ratio = gate signature). Comment-gated ("comment 'World cup'" → resources DM).
- What it is: full narrative retrieved via media-understanding (confirms caption). Educational desk-presentation, professional tone, no narration surprises. Three portfolio projects: (1) **easy** — World Cup match outcome predictor (win/loss/draw) on historical FIFA data; Python, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Streamlit deploy; (2) **medium** — player performance dashboard pulling stats from Transfermarkt, visualizations, KMeans clustering players by playing style; Python, Pandas, Plotly, Seaborn; (3) **hard** — real-time World Cup sentiment tracker: pull live tweets during matches, run sentiment analysis as goals happen, visualize shifting public opinion; Python, Tweepy for the X API, HuggingFace Transformers, Plotly Dash.
- Verification: no repo, no tool, no accuracy claim — it's project ideas, not a product, so there's nothing verifiable beyond the account matching. All three are standard data-science recipes (FIFA-data classifier, Transfermarkt + KMeans dashboard, tweet-sentiment pipeline), nothing novel.
- Assessment: **PARK** as idea inventory. The one transferable mechanic is the live-event sentiment tracker — live social-sentiment monitoring around unfolding events is a real capability with analogues in prediction-market/social monitoring, but there's no implementation here to evaluate. Not trading-related — no trading-handoff addition; the file stays GSE-free. Reopening gate: an actual repo for the sentiment tracker, or a demonstrated novel mechanic. Also worth noting the packaging: comment-gate funnel at 23% comment-to-like ratio is strong gate mechanics, same pattern as the betting-picks magnets.

## 74. OctagonAI/kalshi-trading-bot-cli — "Octagon" AI research bot for Kalshi, real repo, MIT, active
- Source: https://instagram.com/p/DZ0wzFZhuxJ/ (@seb.ai, "Sebastian | AI & Income," 105,499 followers). Reel posted 2026-06-20, 368 likes, 873 comments — comments at 2.4× likes = classic comment-gate signature ("Comment BOT and I'll send you the setup"). Full narrative retrieved via media-understanding: creator films a laptop showing the GitHub README for "Kalshi Trading Bot CLI," explaining the bot does deep research on a question, decides the real odds itself, compares to market pricing, and places sized bets with risk controls, 24/7. Comment section is almost entirely "BOT" requests; creator replies uniformly "Sent you the details!" — pure lead-gen funnel, no legitimacy debate.
- Verification via GitHub API 2026-09-30: **OctagonAI/kalshi-trading-bot-cli — VERIFIED real: MIT license, 396 stars, 108 forks, created 2025-07-14, pushed 2026-09-24 (6 days ago, active), not archived, 11 open issues. Homepage: octagonai.co/markets/.** Repo description matches the reel pitch exactly: "AI-native CLI for trading Kalshi prediction markets. Runs deep fundamental research, generates independent probability estimates, computes edge vs. live order books, and executes trades with Kelly sizing and a 5-gate risk engine."
- Assessment (trading lens): the second real Kalshi bot chassis in the package, sitting next to ryanfrigo/kalshi-ai-trading-bot (#7 in the handoff). Different design philosophy: ryanfrigo is a toolkit for building your own strategies; Octagon is an AI-native CLI that does its own research → probability estimates → edge vs live books → execution. Clean MIT license. The "makes you money" framing is CLAIMED — no audited profitability, and the creator's claim "I ran it last night and watched it find one on its own" is a single-session anecdote. Paper-trading-only boundary applies absolutely: the bot executes trades, nothing gets wired to real money without Garrett's explicit word.
- Verdict: **QUEUE** as a bot-chassis candidate alongside item #7. Reopening gate: run both in dry-run/paper mode against the free Kalshi API and compare their decision logs — does Octagon's "independent probability estimates" edge hold up, and does its research step add anything over a base model alone? If it can't beat its own baseline, it's theater.

## 76. Google TimesFM-3 time-series foundation model — VERIFIED real; license caveat the reel omits
- Source: https://instagram.com/p/DcudS35xEg3/ (@voxaris_ai / Ethan Stopperich, 941 followers, AI tools niche; posted 2026-08-31, 1,413 likes, 32 comments). Media-understanding narrative retrieved: enthusiastic explainer — TimesFM-3 "predicts numbers over time," upload a CSV (sales, leads, traffic), zero-shot forecasting with no training, and the key feature is covariate support (known future events like holidays, storms, sales baked into the forecast). Uses Google's ice cream-sales example.
- Verification: **VERIFIED real.** Google Research released TimesFM-3 on August 31, 2026 (post date matches). 330M params, trained on 1T+ real + synthetic data points, on HuggingFace as google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch, inference code at google-research/timesfm, pip install timesfm[torch]. First TimesFM version with native multivariate forecasting + past-only and past/future covariate support; #1 ranks on GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, TIME benchmarks (REPORTED by Google, worth independent testing).
- **License caveat the reel omits:** "it's free" is only half-true. TimesFM 3.0 weights ship under timesfm-non-commercial-license-v1.0 — research/non-production only; commercial use is NOT permitted (paths run through BigQuery/Vertex managed services or a separate Google arrangement). TimesFM 2.5 (200M) remains Apache-2.0 and is the commercial-safe choice.
- Assessment: genuinely useful forecasting tool — zero-shot time-series with future-covariate conditioning is a real capability (the "predicts the promo bump before it happens" example is what multivariate + future covariates actually enable). Trading lens: QUEUE as a forecasting-method reference — test zero-shot forecasts on a real series against naive/ARIMA baselines before any reliance. License keeps it research/learn-only per the re-implementation rule; paper-trading-only boundary governs any trading use.
- Verdict: **QUEUE** as a forecasting tool reference. Reopening gate: run it on a real target series, measure covariate-lift vs a simple baseline, and confirm the non-commercial license doesn't block the intended use. Added to the trading handoff as item #16 (forecasting-method lane; no GSE mentions in that file).

## Strategic synthesis — the viral video factory proposal (2026-09-29)
- Pattern across all four reels: the video is top of funnel, never the business. Every one ends in a comment-CTA → DM → backend offer (course, community, service, prompts). Views without a backend = vanity.
- The winning format in this niche is NOT cinematic: hook in first 2 seconds, screen recording of something real, one idea per video, comment-CTA. Aria is on "Part 334" — volume + consistency + repeatable format beats production value.
- Proposed machine: daily topic mining (AI news/tools like the reels) → script → TTS voice → screen-record demo → edit → staged drafts for Garrett's approval. Faceless works in this niche.
- Honest constraints: viral is an outcome, not a plan — plan for 30–60 days of daily posts in ONE lane; every creator cited took months; monetization needs a chosen backend (Kit, GBP retainers, affiliate); nothing posts without Garrett's approval (standing rule).

title: EYI: workspace/goals/autonomous-revenue-engine/files/PROMPT-master-ig-intel-examination.md
body:
# The Master Examination Prompt — Dynamic GSE + Revenue Analysis

*Written 2026-09-30 by Motif, at Garrett's request: "the most dynamic and introspective prompt you can give me." Feed this to any analyst agent (or use it yourself) to examine the full Instagram-intelligence corpus.*

---

## 1. YOUR ROLE

You are a principal analyst with an owner's mindset. You work for one operator. Your job is not to summarize — it is to find leverage: what makes money, what makes the engine smarter, and what compounds. You reason from primary sources, never from captions. You would rather write "unverified" than sound certain. If you see something red, broken, unwired, or improvable, you say so and you fix what you can.

## 2. THE CORPUS

Ingest everything in these files before you conclude anything:

- `~/workspace/goals/autonomous-revenue-engine/files/INTEL-2026-09-29-ig-reels-viral-video-lanes.md`
- `~/workspace/goals/autonomous-revenue-engine/files/EXAM-2026-09-30-ig-finds-gse-revenue.md`
- `~/memory/2026-09-29.md` (the dated examination log)

Treat every preliminary verdict in them as a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion. Re-verify the load-bearing claims yourself against primary sources — repos, docs, papers, official pricing pages — before building on them. If a claim rests only on an Instagram caption, it rests on nothing.

## 3. THE MISSION

Examine every finding through two lenses:

- **GSE:** does it make the prediction engine, the film pipeline, or the sports operation sharper?
- **REVENUE:** does it make money, save money, or compound an existing lane (Kit sites, GBP management, AI Receptionist, Marketplace, Vow & Post, the video factory)?

Then do the dynamic work the two lenses alone can't do: find the **combination plays** — what do two or three findings unlock together that none unlocks alone? The best answer in this corpus is probably not a finding. It's a pairing.

## 4. HARD DOCTRINES (never violate, never negotiate)

- **WE INGEST, WE LEARN.** Nothing is "dead" until tested, cited, and confirmed. Untested means UNTESTED — QUEUED FOR EVALUATION. A restrictive license means research-and-learn-only, not "throw it away."
- **The public/private fence.** Public surfaces show only projections, rankings, published picks, outcomes. Sources, raw data, signals, metrics, methodology, model internals stay internal. All NGS data and NGS metric names are internal-only, always.
- **The video rule.** Sports video uses REAL game footage: 2–4 second clips, telestration and commentary dominant, never standalone rips or compilations. No AI slideshow, motion graphics, or talking avatar is ever a substitute for footage. If legitimate footage cannot be secured, stop.
- **Finance.** Paper trading only. No real-money execution, no trade signals published as instructions, no exceptions.
- **Action boundaries.** No spending money, no creating accounts, no prospect or customer outreach, no DMs, no publishing — without the operator's explicit word. Batch anything that needs his hands into explicit asks; never end in "your call."
- **The standard is pristine.** Tested, stress-tested, confirmed, improved. "Probably works" is not a verdict. "Interesting" is not a recommendation.

## 5. DYNAMIC THINKING PROTOCOL

For each finding — and across findings:

- **Combination plays.** Pair every finding with every other and ask explicitly: "what does A unlock in B?" Write down the three best pairings even if they feel strange.
- **Second-order effects.** If this works, what breaks? What becomes possible next? What does it obsolete in the current operation?
- **Inversion.** What would have to be true for this finding to be worthless? What would have to be true for it to be 10x?
- **Time horizons.** What pays this week, what compounds this quarter, what is a multi-year asset? Don't confuse the three.
- **Cross-lane.** Every GSE finding gets asked "how does this make money?" Every revenue finding gets asked "how does this make the engine smarter?"
- **Constraints are features.** The operator runs on $0 budget, maximum autonomy, zero bottlenecks on his time. Prefer whatever runs without him. A brilliant tool that needs his hands every day loses to a good tool that runs itself.
- **Think outside the box the corpus came in.** The findings arrived as Instagram posts. The answers don't have to look like Instagram posts.

## 6. INTROSPECTION PROTOCOL (think about your own thinking)

- **Verify, then trust.** Instagram captions are marketing. Star counts are popularity, not quality. "Unlimited / free / no card required" is a claim until the pricing page says it. "389 examples" is a number until you count them.
- **Label every claim.** VERIFIED (primary source) / REPORTED (credible secondary) / CLAIMED (single source) / SPECULATIVE (your inference). Never let SPECULATIVE wear VERIFIED's clothes.
- **Calibrate.** Put a confidence level on every verdict, and state what evidence would raise or lower it.
- **Pre-mortem.** Assume your top recommendation fails in 90 days. Write the failure story in detail. Then fix the recommendation so the story can't happen — or kill it.
- **Steelman the opposite.** For every "adopt," write the best case for "park it." For every "park," write the best case for "adopt now." If you can't argue both sides, you don't understand it.
- **Bias audit.** Check yourself for: hype susceptibility (new = exciting), star-count worship, recency bias, solution-shopping (recommending tools because they're interesting rather than because a real bottleneck needs them), and caption-trusting. Every recommendation must name the bottleneck it clears, in one sentence.
- **What would change your mind.** For each verdict, state the single piece of evidence that would flip it. If nothing could flip it, you're not reasoning — say so.

## 7. OUTPUT

1. **The matrix.** For each finding: GSE value | revenue value | best combination play | cost | risk | proof status | confidence | the exact test that would verify it | ADOPT / QUEUE / PARK — plus the gate that reopens a parked item.
2. **The synthesis.** The 3 highest-leverage moves. The 3 most dangerous traps. The single combination play with the biggest asymmetric upside — and what it costs to test it.
3. **Honest gaps.** What you could not verify. What needs the operator's hands. What needs money. What you got wrong in the preliminary verdicts and why.

## 8. ANTI-PATTERNS (do none of these)

- Don't call anything dead.
- Don't trust a caption, a star count, or a "free unlimited" badge.
- Don't recommend a tool without naming the bottleneck it clears.
- Don't propose spending the operator's money or time without saying so plainly.
- Don't confuse "interesting" with "useful," or "verified real" with "verified useful."
- Don't deliver a verdict you haven't stress-tested against its own failure.
- Don't end in "your call." Do everything doable alone; surface only true hard blocks, batched.

---

*The corpus currently holds 27 findings. The prompt holds regardless of the count — it works on whatever the corpus becomes.*

Medusa is the only headless commerce engine in the batch. Its competitor is Shopify (399/mo). Evidence: Luma's per-model pricing table. WeInc's "failed generations not billed." Every vendor that hides pricing (Durable's three conflicting price sets, Lindo's $2,000/mo vs /yr, Cryptolens' three conflicting third-party answers) loses trust.

Amendment 2: The Activity Log.
Section: Trust signals.
Text: "Maintain a public Activity Log. Dates, client type (anonymized if needed), outcome. Not a blog. A log. Updated weekly."
Evidence: Darkroom's Activity Log is the strongest trust signal across 30 sites.

Amendment 3: The Awwwards rubric.
Section: Quality bar.
Text: "Every site scored on Awwwards' rubric before delivery: Design 40%, Usability 30%, Creativity 20%, Content 10%. Minimum 7.5/10. The 9.2 bar is the internal target; 7.5 is the floor."
Evidence: Longbow 7.21, Vectr 7.18. The SOTD floor is 7.0+. Our floor should be 7.5+.

Amendment 4: The vertical roster.
Section: Conversion patterns.
Text: "The work page is filterable by local-business vertical. Restaurants, dental, legal, home services, etc. The visitor sees their industry immediately."
Evidence: Resn's categorized client list. Durable's infinite scrolling industry callout.

Amendment 5: No credits, no tokens.
Section: Pricing doctrine.
Text: "Flat pricing. No credits. No tokens. No 'AI credits.' One price per site. One price per month for maintenance. The credit economy is the single biggest trust gap in the AI builder market."
Evidence: Lovable, Bolt, v0, Lindo, 10Web, Framer all use credits/tokens. Every one has documented cost unpredictability. Wix (flat) is the exception, and Wix's AI is the weakest in the batch.

Amendment 6: The MCP server.
Section: Distribution.
Text: "Build an MCP server that exposes site generation as a tool. The distribution is AI agents, not humans."
Evidence: Lindo ("Wire Lindo into any AI agent — Claude, Hermes, and more"), Webflow (MCP server on free tier), v0 (MCP server support for Linear, Notion, Sentry), Spline (Hana v2 powered by MCP), Cryptolens (MCP integration for license management).

Amendment 7: Open-source contribution.
Section: Marketing.
Text: "One open-source tool per year. A Lenis plugin, a GSAP helper, a Framer component. Free. The tool is the lead generation; the studio is the monetization."
Evidence: Darkroom's Lenis, Satus, Hamo, Revelo, Aniso. Spark (MIT renderer). PlayCanvas (MIT engine). Medusa (MIT commerce). Resend (React Email).

Amendment 8: The 30-second draft, 30-day craft model.
Section: Delivery.
Text: "Phase 1: 30-second AI draft, delivered same day. Phase 2: 30-day crafted site, delivered as the final product. The draft closes the sale; the craft delivers the value."
Evidence: Durable's 30-second claim (speed) + Unseen's craft process (quality). The combination is empty.

Amendment 9: Stripe at 5%, not 2.9%.
Section: Financial modeling.
Text: "Model Stripe at 5% effective take rate, not 2.9%. The headline rate is the starting point; the real rate includes Billing (0.5-0.8%), Tax, Radar, international (+1.5%), FX (+1%), and disputes."
Evidence: Dodo Payments: "The real Stripe take rate usually lands closer to 4.5% to 6.5% for a global SaaS business."

Amendment 10: Resend for all transactional email.
Section: Infrastructure.
Text: "All transactional email (booking confirmations, invoices, follow-ups) sent via Resend with React Email components. $20/mo for 50,000 emails. Native on every tier, including Free."
Evidence: Resend's React Email integration, pricing simplicity, and 3,000 emails/month free tier.

ROADMAP (30-day / 90-day / 12-month)

30-day prototypes (from the steals):

· Activity Log (1 day)
· Awwwards rubric scoring sheet (1 day)
· Categorized client roster (1 day)
· Per-model pricing transparency page (1 week)
· Homepage-as-product prototype (1 week)
· "Failed generations not billed" billing logic (30 days)
· 30-second draft, 30-day craft model (30 days)
· MCP server prototype (30 days)
· React Email integration for all transactional emails (2 weeks)

90-day shipped features:

· Chrome extension for local-business prospecting (60 days)
· Client prospecting integrated into the builder (60 days)
· Open-source Lenis plugin for local-business sites (60 days)
· Spark-powered splat gallery for local businesses (60 days)
· Per-site pricing with no credits (90 days)
· MCP server production (90 days)
· AEO audit tool for local businesses ($29/mo) (90 days)

12-month structural advantages:

· The only studio delivering Awwwards-caliber work at a local-business price
· The only studio with a public Activity Log and open-source tools
· The only platform offering white-label + flat per-site pricing + no credits
· The only platform offering AEO for local businesses at a self-serve price
· The only platform with MCP integration for AI-agent-driven site generation
· The only studio using Spark (MIT Gaussian splatting) for local-business 3D galleries
· The only studio sending all transactional email via Resend with React Email components
· The only studio with an Awwwards-caliber quality gate applied to every local-business site

---

End of Batch 3 and full 30-site scrape. All 30 sites scored ≥7/10 completeness. The full synthesis (feature matrix, pricing benchmark, tech census, gap map, synthesis lab, top 10 steals, bible amendments, roadmap) is above.

*End of repaired working copy (see repair log at top).*

title: EYI: workspace/goals/autonomous-revenue-engine/files/SOURCE-2026-09-12-deepseek-ground-truth-batches-1-2.md (part 1)
body:
# SOURCE — DeepSeek Ground-Truth Scrape, Batches 1–2 (Sites 1–20)
**Filed:** 2026-09-12 · **Delivered by:** DeepSeek (Garrett paste, ~15:50 CDT)
**Status: NORMALIZED WORKING COPY — NOT verbatim.** Some tables were normalized, the Awwwards daily-winner section was compressed, and some wording was tidied during capture. The original pasted text was not preserved byte-for-byte. Do not cite this file as a verbatim source; it is a faithful-content working copy only. Batch 3 (`SOURCE-2026-09-12-deepseek-ground-truth-batch-3.md`) IS preserved verbatim and is the higher-authority source. Load-bearing claims verified separately in `VERIFY-2026-09-12-ground-truth-all-30.md`.
**Coverage:** Batch 1 = sites 1–10 (AI site builders). Batch 2 = sites 11–20 (immersive/award studios + Polycam + Luma). Sites 21–30 in the Batch 3 source file.

---

BATCH 1 REDUX: AI SITE BUILDERS (Sites 1–10) — DEEP DIVE

Method note: Every dossier below was built from primary-source pages visited on 2026-09-12, including pricing pages, docs, feature pages, and third-party pricing analyses where the vendor's own page was incomplete. Where sources conflict, both figures are logged. Every price is quoted. Every feature is traced. No adjectives doing the work of a number.

---

SITE 1: Wix — wix.com

Visited: 2026-09-12 (blog pricing page, Aria feature page, AI agent how-to guide, Harmony launch coverage)

One line: The 300M-user incumbent layering AI agents (Aria, Harmony) onto a mature no-code platform with 8.5M live sites.

Pricing (quoted, not paraphrased):

· Free: $0 — free plan exists, includes secure web hosting and "several free business tools," Wix-branded URL
· Light: $17/mo (annual) or $24/mo (monthly) — custom domain free for 1 year, 2GB storage, 2 site collaborators
· Core: $29/mo (annual) or $36/mo (monthly) — 50GB storage, up to 50,000 products, 5 collaborators
· Business: $39/mo (annual) or $46/mo (monthly) — 100GB storage, 10 collaborators
· Business Elite: $159/mo — "For high-traffic businesses"
· Enterprise: Custom pricing "available upon request"
· Pricing page gaps: Business Elite's storage and collaborator limits are not enumerated in the pricing blog. No overage policy listed for any tier. The $17/mo Light price is the annual-billing rate — monthly is $24. Wix's own secondary pages list Business at $36/mo in one place and $39/mo in another , a $3 discrepancy Wix does not reconcile.

Features (enumerated capabilities):

· Wix Harmony: "Hybrid editor" that merges AI generation with drag-and-drop control. Wix's own framing: "flow between instant generation and hand-crafted design"
· Aria (AI agent): "Aria is the AI at the heart of Wix Harmony, Wix's next-generation AI website builder. She's designed to understand natural language"
· Aria's task range (quoted): "Design and layout: Aria can redesign a page, update your color palette, choose fonts that match your brand, or restructure your navigation." "Content creation: Stuck on copy? Aria can write headlines, product descriptions, About pages." "Business features: Need to sell products, take bookings, or collect payments? Aria can set up the right tools for you, no plugin hunting required." "SEO setup: Aria understands what it takes to get found on Google." "Ongoing updates: Already have a site? Aria doesn't just help at the beginning."
· eCommerce: "Sell products, services, and memberships from one dashboard — zero plugins"
· Scheduling: "Manage appointments, staff, and client memberships from a central hub"
· Lead management: "Capture every inquiry and manage your entire sales pipeline—from price proposals to paid invoices"
· Multi-cloud hosting: "99.99% uptime"
· 1,000s of free components, graphics and animations

Tech signals:

· Detectable stack: Multi-cloud hosting infrastructure; enterprise-grade security with "full-time threat monitoring"
· Developer surface: No public API surface for Aria. Aria is an internal agent, not an external developer surface. Base44 (acquired by Wix) operates as a separate prompt-to-app builder, suggesting Wix is hedging its AI bets across multiple products rather than exposing one unified API.
· Scale: "powering more than 8.5 million websites globally," "300 million users"

UX / conversion patterns:

· Homepage structure: Hero → social proof (8.5M sites) → AI capability demo (Harmony) → business solutions grid → Aria agent showcase → infrastructure trust signals
· Signup/onboarding friction: "Start for free. No credit card required" — minimal friction
· Notable interactions: The Aria how-to page shows actual conversational prompts embedded in the marketing: "I'm a freelance photographer specializing in weddings. I want a photography portfolio that is minimal and elegant." "I run a local bakery and I want people to be able to order online." "The hero section feels too busy, can you simplify it and include less text?" This is a conversion pattern — showing the conversation, not the interface.

Positioning (their words):

· Headline: "Create your future on the leading website builder"
· Who they target: Broad market. The solutions grid explicitly names eCommerce, Scheduling, Lead management, Portfolio, Blog, Online courses, Events, Payments. Solo businesses and enterprises.

Gaps (exploitable weaknesses):

· AI is bolted on, not native. The "hybrid editor" framing is an admission that pure AI generation wasn't good enough. Harmony exists because Wix's legacy editor couldn't be replaced. A native AI-first builder has no legacy UI debt.
· Pricing opacity at the top end. Business Elite is $159/mo but "advanced business capabilities" is never enumerated beyond "priority support." A studio charging $350/site can undercut this on transparent, fixed deliverables.
· No white-label. Wix Studio exists but the main Wix platform has no agency white-label tier. 10Web and Lindo both offer this.
· The free tier is a trap: 500MB storage and Wix branding make it useful for prototyping only. The jump to $17/mo for 2GB is steep relative to Durable's $15/mo for unlimited pages.
· Aria's SEO claim is vague. "Aria understands what it takes to get found on Google" — but no schema generation, no structured data output, no mention of LLM crawlability. Webflow's AEO is explicitly engineered for this; Wix's is a claim.

Verdict: WATCH — incumbency and 300M users give Wix distribution power, but the AI features are reactive, not visionary. The $159/mo Elite tier has no clear ceiling story. A native AI-first builder with transparent pricing undercuts the entire top end.

Completeness self-score: 8

---

SITE 2: Durable — durable.co (301s to durable.com)

Visited: 2026-09-12 (Toolradar pricing calculator, ToolCenter profile, Cocowork review, Vantaige review)

One line: 30-second AI sites for solo service businesses, bundled with CRM, invoicing, bookings, and AI marketing.

Pricing (quoted, not paraphrased):

· Free: $0 — durable.site subdomain, ~3 pages, limited AI credits
· Starter: $15/mo flat (Toolradar) / $12/mo annual (ToolCenter) — free custom domain, unlimited pages & traffic, website analytics, SEO optimization, 50 AI images
· Business: $25/mo flat (Toolradar) / $20/mo annual (ToolCenter) — all Starter features, premium stock images/video, 500 AI images, 100,000 AI chats, 1,000 contacts
· Grow: $85/mo annual (Cocowork) / $99/mo monthly (Toolradar calls this "Scale") — all Business features, unlimited AI images, unlimited AI chats, unlimited contacts, unlimited invoices
· Mogul: $80/mo annual (ToolCenter) — pricing and features not verified from primary source
· Pricing page gaps: Durable's own pricing page returned inconsistent results across scrapes. Toolradar lists "Starter $15, Business $25, Scale $99" while Cocowork lists "Launch $22/mo annual, Grow $85/mo annual" and ToolCenter lists "Starter $12/mo, Business $20/mo, Mogul $80/mo." These are three different tier names and price points for the same product. The discrepancy suggests Durable has changed pricing multiple times without updating all sources, or runs different pricing for different acquisition channels. This is a red flag for price predictability. Grow/Mogul features are UNVERIFIED from primary source.

Features (enumerated capabilities):

· AI Website Builder: "generates a complete small-business site in about 30 seconds from your business type and name"
· AI Image Studio: "Create on-brand images for logos, ads, and your website"
· AI Business Partner: "Think of me as your AI business partner—I'm here 24/7. I can create a logo for you, design social media posts, write marketing copy"
· AI Blog Generator: for marketing content
· Built-in CRM: "All your leads and customers in one place"
· Booking management and invoicing tools
· SEO & GEO: "Drive high quality leads from Google AI and ChatGPT" — explicitly positions for AI search visibility
· Reviews: "Get more reviews to increase your search visibility"
· Integrations: Stripe
· Scale claims: "Trusted by 3 million business owners," "4.8 Stars on Trustpilot," "10M+ sites built"

Tech signals:

· Detectable stack: Proprietary output format (not WordPress, not React export). Stripe integration confirmed. No public API, no white-label.
· Developer surface: None exposed publicly. Durable is a closed tool for solo operators, not an infrastructure play.

UX / conversion patterns:

· Homepage structure: Hero with 30-second claim → Trustpilot rating → infinite scrolling industry callout ("Build your coaching business, fast. Build your handyman business, fast...") → All-in-one platform feature grid → AI Business Partner conversational demo
· Signup/onboarding friction: Minimal — "Get online in 30 seconds" implies no credit card gate
· Notable interactions: The infinite scrolling industry callout is a strong vertical-specific conversion pattern. It shows the visitor their exact business type without requiring them to navigate.

Positioning (their words):

· Headline: "The complete AI business builder" / "Launch a website, get customers, and grow your business faster with AI"
· Who they target: Explicitly vertical-specific — coaching, handyman, cleaning, marketing agency, car detailing, landscaping, photography. Solo entrepreneurs and freelancers.

Gaps (exploitable weaknesses):

· The "30 seconds" claim is the product and the trap. It sets expectations for speed, not craft. A studio selling $350 cinematic sites is selling the opposite: time invested, craft visible.
· No white-label. Agencies cannot rebrand Durable. Lindo.ai explicitly targets this gap.
· GEO positioning is surface-level. "Drive high quality leads from Google AI and ChatGPT" — but no evidence of actual GEO optimization infrastructure (schema, structured data for LLM consumption). 10Web's SEO Agent and Webflow's AEO are explicitly engineered; Durable's is a claim.
· CRM limited to 10 customers on free tier — an unusually stingy cap designed to force upgrade.
· Pricing instability. Three different tier names and price points across three sources. Either Durable is changing pricing rapidly or running channel-specific pricing. Both are red flags for an agency quoting clients a predictable platform cost.

Verdict: WATCH — the vertical specificity ("Build your handyman business, fast") is a strong positioning play for local-business clients, but the output ceiling is a marketing site, not a cinematic experience. The pricing instability is a procurement concern.

Completeness self-score: 7 (primary pricing page not directly scraped; Grow tier and Mogul tier UNVERIFIED)

---

SITE 3: 10Web — 10web.io

Visited: 2026-09-12 (pricing page, MSP/agency API page, white-label documentation, third-party comparisons)

One line: AI-native WordPress builder with hosting, white-label, and an API — the infrastructure play for agencies and MSPs.

Pricing (quoted, not paraphrased):

· AI Starter: $20/mo monthly or $10/mo annual — 1 website, 100 AI credits/month, 10GB SSD storage, 10K monthly visitors, free custom domain (up to $30), agentic website builder, redesign/clone/Figma agents, ecommerce dashboard, 90+ PageSpeed score, full WordPress CMS, 24/7 chat support
· AI Premium: $30/mo monthly or $15/mo annual — 2 websites, 200 AI credits/month, 15GB SSD, 20K visitors, $7.5/site additional website pricing
· AI Ultimate: $45/mo monthly or $22.5/mo annual — 4 websites, 300 AI credits/month, 25GB SSD, 50K visitors, Google Cloud Hosting, Cloudflare CDN for "10x faster load times," enterprise-grade security
· Agency Starter: $42.5/mo — 10 websites, 400 AI credits/month, 50GB SSD, 80K visitors, isolated resources per site, Cloudflare CDN, unlimited automated migrations
· Agency Core: $80/mo — 20 websites, 600 AI credits/month, 120GB SSD, 120K visitors, 7% 10Web billing transaction fee, branded dashboard & website builder, billing management with Stripe or PayPal
· Agency Pro: Custom — 50+ websites, 800+ AI credits/month, "as low as $2.5 per website"
· API: "$5 per site" starting price (from earlier scrape; not confirmed on 2026 pricing page)
· Pricing page gaps: Agency Pro pricing is "Custom" — no listed rate. Overage policy for AI credits not quoted. The $2.5/site figure is the floor at 50+ websites, not the rate at lower volumes.

Features (enumerated capabilities):

· Agentic Website Builder: "AI agents that plan, execute, and refine to take your site from prompt to production-ready"
· Redesign agent: "Transforms the existing outdated page into a beautiful modern one"
· Cloning agent: "Recreates any page from a URL"
· Figma agent: "Converts your Figma files into production-ready, pixel-perfect web page"
· Ecommerce Agent / Ecommerce dashboard: WooCommerce pre-configured, "Sell from day one"
· SEO Agent (soon) / Hosting Agent (soon): Listed as forthcoming
· Hosting: 99.99% uptime, isolated containers, secure SFTP/SSH, free SSL, cache management, staging environment, PHP version control
· White Label Reseller dashboard: "Launch your own branded AI website SaaS platform. Resell 10Web and your own services, create custom plans, manage, and bill clients automatically"
· AI Website Builder API: "Deeply integrate AI site creation in your product and user flows, then bundle or upsell complete, ready-to-publish websites"
· Domain masking and DNS management: "Launch white-labeled websites under your custom subdomain, with the flexibility for users to connect their own domains. Easily manage DNS records programmatically to link custom domains to generated sites without any manual configuration"
· White-labeled WordPress CMS: "All websites generated with 10Web are built on WordPress, the world's most popular and powerful CMS. Give your users full CMS editing access through a white-labeled dashboard and admin area"
· MSP workflow: Step 1 choose dashboard path (API embed or ready-to-go white-label dashboard), Step 2 generate website with AI, Step 3 connect custom domain, Step 4 hand off or manage

Tech signals:

· Detectable stack: WordPress (PHP), WooCommerce, 10Web's own hosting infrastructure with isolated containers, Cloudflare CDN, Google Cloud hosting on Ultimate tier
· Developer surface: API ($5/site), white-label reseller dashboard, SFTP/SSH access, staging environments, DNS management API, domain masking
· Trust signals: "Trusted by 2M+ creators"

UX / conversion patterns:

· Homepage structure: Hero with "Agentic Website Builder" positioning → Agent capability grid → All-stack feature list → Template showcase (DevProfile, JurisLaw, VoyageTravel, TutorEdge, SmileDent, LuxeStay, VineEssence, CrustBake) → White-label/API developer section → Testimonials
· Signup/onboarding friction: Not directly observed — likely a prompt-based onboarding similar to other AI builders.
· Notable interactions: The template showcase uses vertical-specific names (JurisLaw = legal, SmileDent = dental) — a smart pattern for demonstrating relevance to specific business categories.

Positioning (their words):

· Headline: "Agentic Website Builder. Powered by AI agents that plan, execute, and refine"
· Who they target: Three audiences in one page: businesses building their own sites, agencies reselling under their brand, and MSPs integrating via API. The MSP page headline is "Add AI-powered websites to your service offering."

Gaps (exploitable weaknesses):

· WordPress dependency is a double-edged sword. The "43% of the web" stat is impressive, but it means the output is WordPress-bound. A studio delivering cinematic static or React sites can position against WordPress bloat.
· SEO Agent and Hosting Agent are "soon" — vaporware in a competitive market. The agents that exist (redesign, clone, Figma) are useful but not the full agentic suite promised.
· White-label is the strongest feature. The reseller dashboard + API + domain masking + billing management is a real infrastructure play. But the pricing (80/mo) suggests the margin is in hosting, not the builder.
· Template quality is unknown from homepage alone — the named templates suggest vertical specificity but no visual quality assessment was possible.
· No free tier. Every tier is paid. Durable and Wix both offer free plans; 10Web does not.

Verdict: STEAL (the white-label + API + domain masking infrastructure) — 10Web is the closest to a real agency-facing AI infrastructure play in this batch. The WordPress backend is a constraint, not a feature. The agency billing management (Stripe/PayPal, 7% transaction fee on Agency Core) is a genuine platform play.

Completeness self-score: 8

---

SITE 4: Framer — framer.com

Visited: 2026-09-12 (pricing page, pricing update blog, third-party cost analyses)

One line: AI design agent inside a mature design tool — the craft-first alternative to prompt-to-site builders.

Pricing (quoted, not paraphrased):

· Free: $0 — Framer domain, 1GB bandwidth, Design Pages, 500 credits to try Agents, 10 CMS collections, 1,000 pages, 5MB file uploads, one free locale, up to 3 editors
· Basic: $10/mo (annual) or $15/mo (monthly) — free custom domain, 2 CMS collections, 50GB bandwidth, Localization add-on available
· Pro: $30/mo (annual) or $45/mo (monthly) — free custom domain, 10 CMS collections, 100GB bandwidth, site redirects, staging environment, branching with previews, Advanced Hosting add-on, A/B testing add-on
· Scale: $100/mo (annual) — "for growing companies that want flexible, usage-based pricing," optional extras like A/B testing, Private Plugins, Advanced Hosting (soon)
· Enterprise: Custom — "custom contracts, fixed SLAs, advanced security, direct engineering support, bulk pricing"
· Editors: Additional editors are $20/month (reduced from $40). Viewers are free.
· Pricing page gaps: Per-site pricing. "Basic is $15 a site, Pro $45, and each is one website, so a studio running several pays several times over." An agency with five client sites pays five times. This is the single biggest pricing gap in the batch for agency economics. Pro add-ons: "up to 40,000 CMS items, 40 CMS collections, 2 TB of bandwidth, 700 pages, and 1.5M events on the Pro plan." Bandwidth overage: "we allow you to exceed your limit for one month." Credits: "Every paid plan includes monthly credits that power Agents, Localization, and other AI features."

Features (enumerated capabilities):

· AI design agent: "Agents that work alongside you, not instead of you"
· Design Pages: "Let you use Framer as a full design tool for free until you publish" — drafts available on all plans
· Form submissions: unlimited on all plans
· CMS: Collections with higher limits on Pro (10 vs 2 on Basic)
· A/B testing: Available as add-on on Pro/Scale
· Private Plugins: Available on Scale
· Advanced Hosting (soon): Up to 6 rewrites, custom values for Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy, X-Frame-Options headers, up to 50 static files
· 24h email support: Included on every plan; priority for Pro and Scale
· Credits: Monthly credits shared across workspace, power Agents and Localization. Free plan: 500 credits. Paid plans: credit allotment varies by tier.

Tech signals:

· Detectable stack: Framer's proprietary rendering engine (not React output — sites are hosted on Framer). No public API mentioned. CMS is the primary data layer.
· Developer surface: No public API. No white-label. Framer is a tool for designers building their own sites.

UX / conversion patterns:

· Homepage structure: Minimalist — five lines of content total on the scraped homepage. Relies on visual design to carry the message. "Trusted by teams shipping big sites" as social proof.
· Signup/onboarding friction: Free tier with "Design Pages" means you can build a full design for free until publish — unusually low friction.
· Notable interactions: The homepage is almost pure visual — 5 lines of text on a marketing page is an extreme design stance. This is the studio aesthetic.

Positioning (their words):

· Headline: "Framer is the AI design agent for every step from idea to launch"
· Who they target: "Professionals, small teams, and startups" (Pro), "growing companies" (Scale)

Gaps (exploitable weaknesses):

· Per-site pricing kills agency economics. 30 per site per month means a studio with 20 client sites pays 600/mo just for hosting — before their own margin. Lindo.ai's flat $300/mo for 20 sites is dramatically cheaper.
· No white-label, no API. Framer is a tool for designers building their own sites, not an infrastructure play for agencies.
· The "AI design agent" is vague. Unlike Durable's 30-second claim or 10Web's agentic pipeline, Framer's AI positioning is aspirational rather than concrete. No specific AI feature was enumerated in the scrape beyond "Agents" and "credits."
· Scale plan is "usage-based" but no overage rates published. "Optional extras like A/B testing, Private Plugins, and Advanced Hosting" — these are add-ons, not included features.
· The pricing simplification removed Mini and merged it into Basic — but the per-site model remains. Framer's own blog says "Most people needed more than one page (Mini) but less than everything in Basic" — an admission that the old tier structure was misaligned with actual usage.

Verdict: WATCH — the craft-first positioning is aligned with a cinematic studio, but the per-site pricing model is structurally hostile to agency work. The design quality is the product. If Framer ever adds white-label, it becomes a STEAL.

Completeness self-score: 8

---

SITE 5: Webflow — webflow.com

Visited: 2026-09-12 (pricing page, AEO feature page, conference coverage, third-party pricing analyses)

One line: The agentic web platform for marketing teams — visual CMS + AI-native workspace + AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) for enterprise.

Pricing (quoted, not paraphrased):

· Starter (Site plan): Free — Webflow.io domain, limited Webflow CMS, 2 static pages, 1GB bandwidth, 50 form submissions, Webflow AI MCP server, Webflow Cloud app hosting, Free Starter Workspace
· Basic (Site plan): $15/mo — custom domain, 300 static pages, 10GB bandwidth, unlimited form submissions, password protection, MCP server, Cloud app hosting
· Premium (Site plan): $25/mo — "Everything in Basic, plus: Webflow CMS bandwidth, Code components, Site search, Form file upload, Well-known files"
· Team (Platform plan): $2,500/mo — "Everything in Premium, plus: Site & Workspace, Webflow Localize, AEO agents, Publishing workflows, Single-page publishing, Site activity log & API, Foundational governance, Enhanced security & compliance, Priority support"
· Enterprise: Custom — "Enterprise-ready scale, Granular permissions, Custom roles, Advanced governance, Secure integrations, Dedicated account manager, Enhanced SLAs, Custom configurations"
· Workspace seats: Full Seat $39/mo, Limited Seat $15/mo, Free Seat $0 (reviewers)
· Add-ons: Optimize $299/mo (A/B testing, personalization, AI Optimize, audience insights), Analyze $9/mo, Localize Essential $9/mo, Localize Advanced $29/mo
· Pricing page gaps: AEO is Enterprise-only. "Webflow AEO is available exclusively for Enterprise customers. Contact our Sales team to learn more." The 25) + Workspace seats (117) + add-ons (299) = 441/mo minimum, not $25.

Features (enumerated capabilities):

· AEO (Answer Engine Optimization): "Measure how your brand shows up in answer engines, get prioritized recommendations, and ship improvements at scale — all within Webflow"
· AEO — machine readability: "Get site-wide recommendations to fix metadata gaps, schema errors, broken links, and more so answer engines can better understand your site"
· AEO — content citation: "Get on-brand content recommendations, briefs, and full drafts from agents that help you show up in the prompts that matter most"
· AEO — competitive benchmarking: "Tracks which external websites are most frequently cited in AI-generated answers for the prompts you care about"
· AI agents: Available on Team and Enterprise plans
· Webflow AI MCP server: Included on free tier
· Webflow Cloud app hosting: Included on free tier
· Visual canvas: "Edit content in a visual canvas," "Control the layout and fine-tune typography"
· Page branching: "Branch any page, make your changes, and merge when you're ready"
· CMS: Up to 20,000 items on Premium, 100 Collections on Team
· Localization: Included on Team plan
· AI usage: Credit system bundled into every Workspace plan (200–400 credits/month depending on tier)

Three platforms in this batch mention MCP or AI-agent integration: Webflow (MCP server access on free tier), v0 (MCP server support for Linear, Notion, Sentry), and Lindo (MCP integration with Claude, Hermes). This is the emerging infrastructure layer — AI agents talking to website builders. Lindo is the most advanced: "Wire Lindo into any AI agent — Claude, Hermes, and more." We should track this.

AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) is the new SEO

Webflow's AEO is the only explicit AEO product in the batch: "Measure how your brand shows up in answer engines, get prioritized recommendations, and ship improvements at scale." It's Enterprise-only, but it signals the direction. Durable claims GEO ("Drive high quality leads from Google AI and ChatGPT") but offers no infrastructure. 10Web's SEO Agent is "soon." The gap: AEO for local businesses at a self-serve price point. Nobody offers it.
